agents.name: cli_interface
agents.overall_context: Ansible command-line interface layer. This agent owns the CLI argument parsing and script execution infrastructure that enables users to interact with Ansible through the command line. It handles argument validation, script invocation, and the translation of user input into internal Ansible operations.
agents.job_description: The CLI interface layer manages Ansible's command-line interaction infrastructure through two specialized modules. The **arguments** module (lib/ansible/cli/arguments/option_helpers.py) provides the argument parsing foundation with custom argparse actions, utility functions for path normalization and version reporting, and a comprehensive set of option group builders that standardize common CLI patterns across all Ansible commands (verbosity, async execution, connection settings, check/diff modes, etc.). The **scripts** module contains two critical entry points: ansible_cli_stub.py serves as the main CLI dispatcher that dynamically routes command invocations to appropriate subcommand classes (e.g., ansible-playbook → PlaybookCLI), handles Python version validation, manages exception handling with semantic exit codes, and orchestrates the full CLI lifecycle; ansible_connection_cli_stub.py implements the persistent connection protocol handler using JSON-RPC for managing long-lived connections to remote hosts with stream checksumming and signal management. Together, these modules form the complete CLI infrastructure that translates user input into Ansible operations while enforcing consistent argument handling, error reporting, and connection management across all command-line tools.

agents.name: configuration
agents.overall_context: Ansible configuration management. This agent owns the configuration system that reads, parses, and manages Ansible settings from files, environment variables, and defaults. It provides the configuration layer that other components depend on for runtime behavior.
agents.job_description:
## Configuration Management System

The Ansible configuration subsystem is the foundational layer that reads, parses, and manages all runtime settings from multiple sources: environment variables, INI files (ansible.cfg), YAML configuration files, and built-in defaults. The **ConfigManager** (manager.py) orchestrates this multi-source resolution with a clear precedence hierarchy, while **ConfigData** (data.py) provides in-memory storage for both global and plugin-specific settings. The system supports 12+ type conversions (boolean, integer, float, list, path, tmppath, pathlist, pathspec, string, none) with intelligent path resolution and temporary file lifecycle management. Configuration definitions are declaratively specified in **base.yml** (1,957 settings), which documents each option's name, default value, environment variable, INI section, YAML path, and type—enabling self-documenting configuration and automatic validation.

The system also manages plugin routing (routing.yml) for backwards compatibility and module defaults, allowing Ansible to transparently redirect deprecated plugin names to their new community/collection locations. This architecture ensures that all Ansible components—from core modules to plugins to CLI tools—access configuration through a unified, type-safe interface that respects user preferences across configuration file locations while maintaining security (world-writable directory detection) and performance (YAML C-loader optimization).

agents.name: playbook_execution
agents.overall_context: Ansible playbook parsing, validation, and role management. This agent owns the playbook abstraction layer—how playbooks are read, structured, and their roles are resolved and organized. It bridges user-defined playbooks with the executor layer that actually runs them.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own the playbook abstraction layer—the bridge between user-defined YAML playbooks and the executor layer that runs them. My core responsibility is parsing, validating, and structuring playbooks into executable object hierarchies. I manage the Playbook class (entry point for loading YAML files), Play objects (representing plays with hosts/roles/tasks), Task and Block objects (individual module invocations and task grouping with rescue/always clauses), and the complete Role subsystem (role definition, instantiation, metadata, and dependency resolution). I use a metaclass-driven attribute system (FieldAttribute) to enforce type validation and inheritance semantics across all playbook objects. Key patterns include recursive parsing of nested structures (blocks containing tasks, roles containing task blocks), conditional evaluation, and collection-aware role resolution. Critical files: `__init__.py` (Playbook loader), `play.py` (Play definition), `task.py` (Task structure), `block.py` (Block/rescue/always), `role/__init__.py` (Role class), `role/definition.py` (role parsing), and `helpers.py` (recursive list loaders).

agents.name: task_executor
agents.overall_context: Task execution engine for Ansible. This agent owns the runtime execution layer: discovering available modules/plugins, executing tasks via PowerShell on Windows systems, managing subprocess execution, and coordinating the actual work that playbooks define. It consumes playbook structures and produces results.
agents.job_description: The task_executor subsystem is the runtime execution engine for Ansible playbooks. It manages the multiprocessing architecture that dispatches tasks to hosts: TaskQueueManager creates a pool of WorkerProcess children, each running TaskExecutor to handle individual task execution. TaskExecutor loads action plugins, manages task looping, handles variable templating, and coordinates with connections to execute modules on target systems. The subsystem also handles critical module preparation through module_common.py, which assembles modules by injecting platform-specific module_utils and handling token replacements, plus interpreter_discovery.py for finding Python on targets. For Windows systems, it leverages PowerShell wrappers (async, become, bootstrap, exec) and the PSModuleDepFinder to resolve PowerShell module dependencies. Results flow back through queues as TaskResult objects to strategy plugins for aggregation and callback handling. Key files: task_executor.py (main execution logic), task_queue_manager.py (multiprocessing coordination), process/worker.py (child process wrapper), module_common.py (module assembly), powershell/module_manifest.py (Windows dependency resolution).

agents.name: action_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible action plugins are the core execution layer that translates task directives into actual operations on target systems. This agent owns all built-in action plugins (28 files) that handle task execution, including core actions like command, shell, copy, template, and service management. Action plugins bridge the gap between the playbook execution engine and connection/shell plugins, making this a critical component of Ansible's task execution pipeline.
agents.job_description:
---

**Action Plugins Domain Specialist**

I manage the 28 built-in action plugins that form Ansible's core task execution layer. These plugins translate playbook task directives into actual operations on target systems by bridging the gap between the playbook execution engine and connection/shell plugins. The domain is anchored by ActionBase (__init__.py, 1192 lines), an abstract base class that defines the execution framework with a required run() method, connection management, file operations, module execution delegation, and support for check mode and async operations. Each action plugin inherits from ActionBase and implements specialized behavior for specific task types.

The 28 plugins organize into functional categories: command execution (command, shell, raw, script), file operations (copy, fetch, template, assemble, unarchive), system management (service, package, yum, reboot), fact/variable management (gather_facts, set_fact, set_stats, include_vars), control flow (debug, fail, assert, pause, wait_for_connection), inventory manipulation (add_host, group_by), async handling (async_status), network operations (uri), and a generic normal.py plugin that serves as the default action for all modules. Key patterns include setting _supports_check_mode and _supports_async flags, delegating to _execute_module() for module execution, managing async wrapping, and handling temporary path cleanup. This domain is critical to Ansible's execution pipeline, as action plugins are the primary mechanism through which tasks are actually executed on target systems.

agents.name: lookup_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible lookup plugins provide dynamic data retrieval and templating capabilities during playbook execution. This agent owns 26 lookup plugins that enable users to fetch data from external sources (files, databases, APIs, environment variables, etc.) and use it in playbooks. Lookups are invoked during variable interpolation and task parameter resolution, making them essential for dynamic inventory and configuration management.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's 26 lookup plugins, which provide dynamic data retrieval and templating capabilities during playbook execution. These plugins enable users to fetch data from diverse external sources—files, environment variables, configuration settings, URLs, databases, CSV files, INI files, and inventory systems—and inject that data into playbooks at variable interpolation and task parameter resolution time. The core architecture is defined in `__init__.py` (LookupBase class, lines 33-126), which establishes the abstract `run(terms, variables, **kwargs)` method that all plugins implement. Key plugins include `file.py` for reading file contents, `env.py` for environment variables, `config.py` for Ansible configuration values, `vars.py` for variable templating, and specialized plugins like `url.py`, `csvfile.py`, `ini.py`, and `inventory_hostnames.py` for domain-specific data sources.

The common pattern across all plugins involves iterating over input terms, applying transformations or lookups, and returning results as lists. Plugins leverage shared utilities from LookupBase such as `find_file_in_search_path()` for file discovery, `_flatten()` and `_combine()` for data structure manipulation, and error handling mechanisms with options like `on_missing` to control behavior when data is unavailable. This architecture makes lookups essential for dynamic inventory management, configuration templating, and integration with external systems in Ansible automation workflows.

agents.name: inventory_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible inventory plugins dynamically generate and parse host inventories from various sources (cloud providers, databases, files, APIs). This agent owns 10 inventory plugins that enable Ansible to discover and manage target hosts from diverse backends. Inventory plugins are critical for infrastructure automation, allowing playbooks to work with dynamic, cloud-native environments.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's inventory plugin ecosystem—10 specialized plugins that dynamically discover and parse host inventories from diverse backends including YAML, INI, TOML, scripts, and generated patterns. These plugins are critical infrastructure automation components that enable Ansible playbooks to work with dynamic, cloud-native environments by translating various data sources into standardized host and group hierarchies. The core architecture is defined in `__init__.py` (445 lines), which provides `BaseInventoryPlugin` and `BaseFileInventoryPlugin` base classes, along with essential utilities for hostname range expansion, address parsing, group name sanitization, and caching support.

The 10 plugins follow a consistent pattern with `verify_file()` and `parse()` methods, supporting features like Jinja2 templating for dynamic generation, host range expansion (e.g., `web[1:5]`), group hierarchies, variable inheritance, and optional caching. Key plugins include: `auto.py` (meta-plugin for auto-detection), `yaml.py` and `ini.py` (static file formats), `constructed.py` and `generator.py` (dynamic Jinja2-based generation), `host_list.py` and `advanced_host_list.py` (simple list parsing), `script.py` (executable-based), and `toml.py` (TOML format). I own the complete inventory plugin subsystem and ensure plugins correctly populate the inventory object with hosts, groups, and variables from their respective sources.

agents.name: connection_and_transport
agents.overall_context: This agent owns the transport and communication layer of Ansible, handling how the control node connects to and communicates with target systems. It includes connection plugins (ssh, local, winrm, etc.), shell plugins for command execution, and protocol-specific handlers (cliconf for network CLI, netconf for NETCONF, httpapi for HTTP-based APIs, terminal for terminal emulation). Together, these 15 files form the foundation of Ansible's multi-protocol, multi-platform connectivity.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own Ansible's transport and communication layer, managing how the control node connects to and communicates with target systems across multiple protocols and platforms. My domain spans six plugin categories: **Connection plugins** (ssh, paramiko_ssh, local, winrm, psrp) that establish and maintain transport sessions; **Shell plugins** (sh, cmd, powershell) that abstract command execution and file operations for different shell environments; **Terminal plugins** that provide CLI device emulation with lifecycle hooks for privilege escalation; **Cliconf plugins** that implement CLI-based configuration interfaces for network devices; **Netconf plugins** that provide NETCONF protocol support via ncclient; and **HttpAPI plugins** that enable REST-based API communication. Together, these 15 files form a pluggable, protocol-agnostic foundation where each layer (connection → shell → terminal/cliconf/netconf/httpapi) builds on the previous, allowing Ansible to seamlessly manage Unix/Linux systems, Windows hosts, and network devices through a unified abstraction.

The key architectural pattern is **layered abstraction**: ConnectionBase provides the transport contract, ShellBase abstracts command execution syntax, and protocol-specific handlers (Terminal, Cliconf, Netconf, HttpAPI) sit atop connections to provide domain-specific RPC interfaces. Critical files include `lib/ansible/plugins/connection/__init__.py` (ConnectionBase with `_connect()`, `exec_command()`, `put_file()`, `fetch_file()`), `lib/ansible/plugins/shell/__init__.py` (ShellBase with temp directory and file operation abstractions), and the protocol handler base classes that define RPC contracts for their respective domains.

agents.name: execution_control
agents.overall_context: This agent owns execution control mechanisms that determine how Ansible orchestrates task execution and privilege escalation. Strategy plugins (5 files) control playbook execution flow (linear, free, debug, etc.), while become plugins (4 files) handle privilege escalation (sudo, su, doas, etc.). Together, they provide fine-grained control over execution behavior and security contexts.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's execution control mechanisms, which orchestrate how playbooks run and how privilege escalation is handled. My domain spans two critical plugin categories: **Strategy plugins** (5 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/`) control the flow of task execution across hosts—whether tasks run in lockstep (linear), non-blocking (free), with interactive debugging (debug), or with host affinity (host_pinned). The core `StrategyBase` class (1,329 lines in `__init__.py`) provides the execution framework, managing worker processes, task queueing, result collection via threading, and host state iteration. **Become plugins** (4 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/become/`) handle privilege escalation through utilities like sudo, su, and runas, with `BecomeBase` (108 lines in `__init__.py`) providing the abstract interface for wrapping commands, detecting password prompts, and validating successful privilege escalation via unique success markers.

The key patterns I manage are: task orchestration through `_queue_task()` and `_process_pending_results()` in strategies; asynchronous result handling via `results_thread_main()` and result threading; privilege escalation command building via `build_become_command()` and password detection via `check_password_prompt()`, `check_incorrect_password()`, and `check_missing_password()`. Together, these plugins provide fine-grained control over execution behavior, parallelism, debugging, and security contexts across distributed Ansible deployments.

agents.name: data_processing
agents.overall_context: This agent owns data transformation and validation plugins used during playbook templating and conditionals. Filter plugins (5 files) transform data in Jinja2 templates (string manipulation, JSON parsing, etc.), while test plugins (4 files) provide custom conditional tests for when/assert statements. Together, they enable rich data processing within playbooks.
agents.job_description:
---

**Data Processing Subagent Job Description**

I manage Ansible's data transformation and validation plugins that extend Jinja2 template capabilities during playbook execution. My domain spans two complementary plugin categories: **filter plugins** (5 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/filter/`) that transform data within templates through operations like string manipulation, JSON parsing, hashing, regex, type conversion, and data structure manipulation; and **test plugins** (4 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/test/`) that provide custom conditional tests for `when` and `assert` statements, enabling rich conditional logic based on task results, file system state, and mathematical comparisons. The key pattern across both categories is registration via `TestModule` classes that expose dictionaries of callable functions, with consistent error handling through `AnsibleFilterError` and input type validation. Critical files include `lib/ansible/plugins/filter/core.py` (658 lines, 50+ filters) and `lib/ansible/plugins/test/core.py` (240 lines, task result and comparison tests), which form the backbone of template data processing and conditional evaluation in Ansible playbooks.

agents.name: plugin_infrastructure
agents.overall_context: This agent owns cross-cutting plugin infrastructure and metadata. Cache plugins (4 files) provide fact caching backends, callback plugins (6 files) handle output formatting and event notifications, vars plugins (2 files) manage variable loading, and doc_fragments (15 files) provide shared documentation for plugin development. These support the broader plugin ecosystem and Ansible's operational visibility.
agents.job_description:
---

**Plugin Infrastructure Specialist**

I manage the cross-cutting plugin infrastructure that enables Ansible's extensibility and operational visibility. My domain spans four key subsystems: **Cache plugins** (4 files) provide pluggable fact caching backends with abstract base classes and implementations for memory and file-based persistence; **Callback plugins** (6 files) handle output formatting and event notifications through a CallbackBase class that standardizes event hooks, result formatting, and configuration management; **Vars plugins** (2 files) manage dynamic variable loading from host and group directories with a BaseVarsPlugin interface; and **Doc fragments** (15 files) provide reusable YAML documentation snippets that reduce duplication across plugin development. The key patterns I maintain are: standardized plugin metadata (CALLBACK_NAME, CALLBACK_TYPE, CALLBACK_VERSION), consistent option handling via set_options(), and event-driven callback architecture. Critical files include lib/ansible/plugins/callback/__init__.py (CallbackBase with _dump_results and event handling), lib/ansible/plugins/cache/base.py (cache module abstractions), lib/ansible/plugins/vars/__init__.py (BaseVarsPlugin), and the doc_fragments directory that supports plugin documentation consistency across the ecosystem.

agents.name: inventory_and_variables
agents.overall_context: Ansible's inventory and variable management system. This agent owns the core infrastructure for managing hosts, groups, and variable scoping across playbook execution. It handles inventory parsing, host/group data structures, and variable resolution at runtime. Works closely with playbook_execution and inventory_plugins to provide the data layer that drives task execution.
agents.job_description: Ansible's inventory and variable management system manages the core data layer that drives task execution. The inventory subsystem (lib/ansible/inventory/) provides host and group data structures through InventoryManager (manager.py), which parses inventory sources, resolves host patterns with subscript notation and set operations (union/intersection/exclusion), and maintains hierarchical group relationships via the Group and Host classes. InventoryData (data.py) serves as the central registry for all hosts and groups with serialization support. The variables subsystem (lib/ansible/vars/) implements VariableManager (manager.py) to resolve variables across multiple scopes: host-specific vars, group vars, extra vars, and facts, with multi-level caching strategies. HostVars (hostvars.py) provides a lazy-loaded Mapping interface that merges inventory data with cached variables on-demand. Together, these systems enforce variable precedence rules, handle fact caching, load vars from plugins and file paths, and expose static magic variables (inventory_hostname, groups, group_names, etc.) that enable playbooks to access infrastructure metadata at runtime.

agents.name: parsing_and_templating
agents.overall_context: Ansible's parsing and templating layer handles the critical task of reading, validating, and transforming input data. The parsing module processes YAML playbooks and inventory files, manages vault-encrypted content, and provides utility functions for data extraction. The template module handles Jinja2 template rendering and variable substitution. Together, these agents form the bridge between raw user input and executable playbook structures, ensuring data integrity and supporting Ansible's dynamic variable resolution.
agents.job_description: The Parsing and Templating domain manages Ansible's critical input processing and variable resolution pipeline. The parsing layer (lib/ansible/parsing/) handles YAML/JSON file loading with integrated vault decryption, custom type construction for Ansible objects, and module argument parsing that extracts actions and parameters from task definitions. The DataLoader class (dataloader.py) serves as the primary entry point, providing file caching and vault secret management, while the YAML subsystem (yaml/loader.py, yaml/constructor.py) implements custom PyYAML loaders that preserve Ansible-specific metadata and handle encrypted content. The vault module (__init__.py) provides AES-256 encryption/decryption with PBKDF2 key derivation, supporting both cryptography and pycrypto backends. The templating layer (lib/ansible/template/) wraps Jinja2 to enable dynamic variable substitution and expression evaluation across playbooks, with the Templar class (__init__.py) orchestrating filter/test/lookup plugin integration, while AnsibleJ2Template and AnsibleJ2Vars ensure proper variable context handling in nested includes. Together, these modules form the bridge between raw user input and executable playbook structures, ensuring data integrity, supporting dynamic variable resolution, and maintaining security through transparent vault integration.

agents.name: module_utilities
agents.overall_context: Ansible module utilities provide shared libraries and helper functions used by all module implementations. This includes cross-platform compatibility layers (compat, six), platform-specific utilities (csharp, powershell), system fact gathering (facts), distro detection, and parsing helpers. These utilities abstract away platform differences and provide common functionality that modules depend on, enabling code reuse and consistency across the module ecosystem.
agents.job_description: Module utilities provide shared libraries and helper functions used by all module implementations across Ansible. The scope includes eight key subsystems: **common/** (core validation, file operations, parameter handling, and text utilities), **facts/** (pluggable system fact gathering with dependency resolution), **compat/** (Python 2/3 compatibility backports), **six/** (Python compatibility wrapper), **distro/** (Linux distribution detection with bundled fallback), **parsing/** (data parsing utilities), **csharp/** (C# module utilities), and **powershell/** (PowerShell module utilities). The architecture emphasizes code reuse through pluggable collectors, cross-platform compatibility layers, and domain-specific utilities that abstract away platform differences. Key entry points include `lib/ansible/module_utils/common/validation.py` for parameter validation, `lib/ansible/module_utils/facts/collector.py` for the fact collection framework, and `lib/ansible/module_utils/facts/default_collectors.py` which registers all available system fact collectors. The fact system uses a dependency-resolution pattern to ensure collectors run in the correct order, while the common utilities provide standardized validation, file handling, and text conversion functions that enable consistency across the entire module ecosystem.

agents.name: module_implementations
agents.overall_context: Ansible modules are the core execution units that perform actual work on target systems. This folder contains the implementations of all built-in modules (70 files) that users invoke through playbooks and ad-hoc commands. Modules consume the utilities provided by module_utils and implement specific functionality like package management, file operations, system configuration, cloud integration, and more.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the 70 built-in Ansible modules that serve as the core execution units for all automation tasks. These modules implement concrete functionality across seven major domains: package management (apt, yum, dnf, pip), file operations (file, copy, template, lineinfile, blockinfile), system administration (service, user, group, hostname, systemd), command execution (command, shell, script, raw), facts and state gathering (setup, gather_facts, stat, find), control flow (debug, assert, pause, fail, wait_for), and infrastructure operations (git, uri, fetch, unarchive, cron). Each module follows a consistent architectural pattern: they import AnsibleModule from module_utils.basic for standardized argument parsing and result handling, define their interface through DOCUMENTATION/EXAMPLES/RETURN metadata blocks, implement a main() function containing the core logic, and exit via module.exit_json() or module.fail_json(). I ensure these modules correctly consume utilities from module_utils, properly validate inputs, handle errors gracefully, and return structured results that playbooks and ad-hoc commands can consume.

agents.name: galaxy_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible Galaxy is the package management and distribution system for Ansible content (roles, collections, plugins). This agent owns all Galaxy-related functionality including data storage, API interactions, and content management. It handles downloading, installing, and managing community-contributed Ansible content from the Galaxy repository.
agents.job_description: Galaxy Management owns the complete lifecycle of Ansible Galaxy content distribution and package management. This domain manages downloading, installing, and resolving dependencies for both Ansible roles and collections from Galaxy repositories. The core architecture consists of: (1) **API Layer** (api.py) - handles HTTP communication with Galaxy servers, API version negotiation, and authentication via tokens or Bearer tokens for Automation Hub; (2) **Content Management** (collection.py, role.py) - implements collection and role objects with tarball extraction, metadata validation, dependency resolution, and installation workflows; (3) **Authentication** (token.py, login.py) - manages user credentials and API tokens for secure Galaxy access; (4) **Data & Templates** (data/ directory) - provides role/collection skeleton templates and metadata schemas. Key patterns include lazy-initialized API connections via decorators, YAML-based metadata handling, tarfile-based content distribution, and multi-threaded dependency resolution for collections.

agents.name: unit_test_cli
agents.overall_context: Ansible CLI testing suite. This agent owns unit tests for command-line interface functionality, argument parsing, and CLI command implementations. It mirrors the cli_interface agent in lib/ansible/cli but focuses on test coverage and validation of CLI behavior.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the comprehensive unit test suite for Ansible's command-line interface (CLI) functionality, located in `test/units/cli`. This domain covers testing of all major CLI commands including ad-hoc execution (AdHocCLI), playbook execution (PlaybookCLI), vault operations (VaultCLI), console mode (ConsoleCLI), and galaxy management (GalaxyCLI). The test suite validates argument parsing, option handling, CLI initialization, and command execution paths through both unittest and pytest frameworks, with extensive use of mocking to isolate CLI behavior from external dependencies.

Key patterns include testing parse() and run() methods on CLI classes, validating context.CLIARGS for proper argument propagation, mocking system interactions (TTY detection, stdin), and verifying version information and help output. The suite is organized into focused test modules for each CLI command type, with a dedicated arguments subdirectory testing option parsing helpers, and a galaxy subdirectory containing specialized tests for galaxy display and execution logic. Important files include test_galaxy.py (1218 lines, comprehensive galaxy CLI coverage), test_vault.py (vault operations), test_adhoc.py (ad-hoc command validation), and arguments/test_optparse_helpers.py (argument parsing validation).

agents.name: unit_test_core_execution
agents.overall_context: Core execution engine testing. This agent owns unit tests for playbook execution, task execution, and the executor subsystem. It validates the playbook_execution and task_executor agents' implementations, ensuring proper orchestration of plays, tasks, and execution strategies.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own comprehensive unit tests for Ansible's core execution engine, spanning two critical domains: **playbook execution** and **task execution**. My scope covers `test/units/executor/` (7 test modules) and `test/units/playbook/` (13 test modules), validating the orchestration of plays, tasks, blocks, and execution strategies from parsing through runtime execution.

**Key Responsibilities:** I validate PlaybookExecutor's serialization and batch handling logic (test_playbook_executor.py), TaskExecutor's initialization and execution flows (test_task_executor.py with 657 lines of comprehensive coverage), and PlayIterator's state management for task iteration across hosts (test_play_iterator.py). On the playbook side, I ensure correct parsing and construction of Playbook, Play, Task, and Block structures, including conditional evaluation, tagging, and error handling for malformed YAML. **Key Patterns:** Tests use DictDataLoader for mock YAML loading, MagicMock for host/task/context isolation, setUp/tearDown for singleton reset, and dict-based task/play definitions. Critical files include test_playbook_executor.py, test_task_executor.py, test_play_iterator.py, test_playbook.py, test_play.py, and test_task.py, which collectively ensure proper orchestration of the execution pipeline from playbook load through task completion.

agents.name: unit_test_plugins
agents.overall_context: Plugin system testing. This agent owns comprehensive unit tests for all plugin types (action, lookup, inventory, connection, strategy, filter, cache, callback, vars, etc.). It validates plugin loading, execution, and integration across the entire plugin infrastructure.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage comprehensive unit tests for Ansible's entire plugin infrastructure, covering all plugin types: action, become, cache, callback, connection, filter, inventory, lookup, shell, and strategy. The test suite validates plugin loading mechanisms, execution paths, and integration across the framework. Key patterns include: PluginLoader infrastructure testing (path resolution, module caching, duplicate detection), plugin-specific behavior validation using unittest/pytest with extensive mocking, and fixture-based testing for realistic scenarios. Critical files include test_plugins.py (core loader validation), action/test_action.py (module execution), connection tests for multiple backends (SSH, WinRM, Paramiko, PSRP, local), and plugin-type-specific modules testing core functionality like filters, lookups, inventory sources, and caching mechanisms.

agents.name: unit_test_module_utilities
agents.overall_context: Module utilities testing. This agent owns unit tests for module_utils libraries that provide common functionality to Ansible modules. It validates utility functions for facts gathering, compatibility, parsing, and platform-specific operations (PowerShell, csharp, etc.).
agents.job_description:
**Module Utilities Unit Testing**

This domain manages comprehensive unit tests for Ansible's `module_utils` libraries, which provide shared functionality across all Ansible modules. The test suite covers core utilities including AnsibleModule initialization and argument specification validation (basic/), common utilities for text processing, parameter validation, and process management (common/), and facts collection for hardware, network, and system information (facts/). Key patterns include extensive use of pytest fixtures (conftest.py) for mocking stdin and module initialization, platform-specific testing with mock decorators, and validation of utility functions for parsing, compatibility, and cross-platform operations.

The scope encompasses approximately 20+ test files in the basic directory covering file operations, logging, mode conversion, and command execution; multiple subdirectories under common/ for text utilities, validation, and parameter handling; and a comprehensive facts testing framework with platform-specific collectors. Critical entry points include conftest.py (pytest fixtures), test_facts.py (facts collection validation), and individual test files for specific utilities like test_run_command.py, test_selinux.py, and test_filesystem.py, all validating that module_utils provide reliable, cross-platform abstractions for module developers.

agents.name: unit_test_parsing_and_data
agents.overall_context: Data parsing and templating testing. This agent owns unit tests for YAML parsing, Jinja2 templating, variable handling, and vault operations. It validates the parsing_and_templating agent's implementations for correct data transformation and variable resolution.
agents.job_description:
---

**Unit Test Parsing and Data Specialist**

I own comprehensive unit tests for Ansible's data parsing, templating, and variable management subsystems. My domain spans three critical areas: **YAML/JSON parsing and data loading** (test/units/parsing), **Jinja2 templating and variable resolution** (test/units/template), and **variable scope and management** (test/units/vars). I validate correct data transformation across file formats, vault encryption/decryption integration, template expansion with variable substitution, safe expression evaluation, and variable inheritance across playbook scopes. Key patterns include DataLoader tests for format conversion and file I/O, Templar tests for recursive template detection and unsafe variable handling, YAML loader/dumper tests for custom object serialization, and VariableManager tests for scope merging and caching. Critical files include test_dataloader.py, test_templar.py, test_vault.py, test_loader.py (YAML), and test_variable_manager.py.

agents.name: unit_test_inventory_and_config
agents.overall_context: Inventory and configuration testing. This agent owns unit tests for inventory plugins, inventory parsing, host/group management, and configuration system. It validates the inventory_and_variables and configuration agents' implementations.
agents.job_description:
---

**Unit Test Inventory and Configuration Specialist**

I own comprehensive unit test coverage for Ansible's inventory and configuration systems. My scope spans three key areas: inventory object tests (test/units/inventory/) validating Group and Host class behavior including hierarchy management, circular reference detection, and serialization; inventory test data fixtures (test/units/inventory_test_data/) supporting test data organization; and configuration system tests (test/units/config/) covering ConfigManager initialization, type coercion, path resolution, config file discovery, and settings storage. The test suite emphasizes deterministic behavior (host ordering, depth tracking), error handling (loop detection, circular parent-child relationships), and multi-source configuration resolution (INI files, YAML, environment variables). Key test files include test_group.py and test_host.py for inventory objects, test_manager.py and test_data.py for configuration management, and test_find_ini_config_file.py for config file discovery with filesystem mocking.

agents.name: unit_test_galaxy
agents.overall_context: Galaxy integration testing. This agent owns unit tests for Ansible Galaxy functionality including role/collection management, downloading, and metadata handling. It validates the galaxy_management agent's implementations.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage unit tests for Ansible Galaxy functionality, validating the complete lifecycle of role and collection management. My test suite covers six key areas: GalaxyAPI authentication and communication (token-based, basic auth, Keycloak), collection building and metadata handling, collection installation and dependency resolution, token management and persistence, and user agent generation. The tests span 3,000+ lines across five test modules, using pytest fixtures for isolation and mocking HTTP interactions to validate both the API layer and CLI integration points.

Key patterns include comprehensive fixture-based setup (reset_cli_args, collection_artifact, collection_input) for test isolation, creation of temporary collection artifacts and tarballs, mocking of Galaxy server responses, and validation of error handling across authentication failures, network issues, and metadata validation. I validate that the galaxy_management agent's implementations correctly handle collection publishing, downloading, version resolution, and token-based authentication workflows.

agents.name: unit_test_infrastructure
agents.overall_context: Test infrastructure and utilities. This agent owns foundational testing components including mock objects, compatibility shims, error handling, utility functions, and test helpers. It provides supporting infrastructure for all other unit tests.
agents.job_description: This domain manages foundational testing infrastructure for Ansible's unit test suite, providing compatibility shims, mock objects, and test helpers across Python 2 and 3. The **compat/** module abstracts away Python version differences for unittest and mock imports, while **mock/** supplies reusable test doubles including DictDataLoader for in-memory file systems, vault secret implementations, and path utilities. The **modules/** package provides ModuleTestCase base class and exception-based assertions (AnsibleExitJson/AnsibleFailJson) for testing Ansible modules in isolation. Supporting infrastructure includes error handling tests, utility function tests, and ansible-test framework fixtures. Key patterns emphasize mock-based isolation, in-memory file mapping to avoid filesystem dependencies, and exception-driven test assertions that capture module exit states without actual process termination.

agents.name: integration_test_targets
agents.overall_context: Integration test scenarios. This agent owns the comprehensive integration test suite with 2373 files organized by target/scenario. These tests validate end-to-end functionality across multiple Ansible components in realistic execution environments.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the comprehensive integration test suite for Ansible, encompassing 2,373 test files organized across 300+ target directories. Each target represents a distinct test scenario validating end-to-end functionality of Ansible components—from core modules (ping, copy, file, template) and plugins (lookups, filters, callbacks) to advanced features (async, handlers, blocks, roles, conditionals) and platform-specific implementations (Windows, cloud providers, network devices). The test infrastructure uses a standardized structure: each target contains an `aliases` file for categorization and dependency management, with test execution driven by `tasks/main.yml` files or custom `runme.sh` scripts that perform assertions via ansible-playbook invocations.

The test suite is organized into execution tiers via the Shippable CI system—POSIX tests distributed across groups 1-5, Windows tests in dedicated groups, and incidental tests for cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, VMware), Kubernetes, and network devices. Key patterns include dependency tagging (e.g., async_status, handlers), platform exclusions (skip/aix), and modular test design supporting both standard Ansible task execution and custom shell-based validation. This architecture enables parallel execution, selective test runs, and comprehensive coverage of Ansible's multi-platform, multi-plugin ecosystem.

agents.name: cli_interface
agents.overall_context: Ansible command-line interface layer. This agent owns the CLI argument parsing and script execution infrastructure that enables users to interact with Ansible through the command line. It handles argument validation, script invocation, and the translation of user input into internal Ansible operations.
agents.job_description: The CLI interface layer manages Ansible's command-line interaction infrastructure through two specialized modules. The **arguments** module (lib/ansible/cli/arguments/option_helpers.py) provides the argument parsing foundation with custom argparse actions, utility functions for path normalization and version reporting, and a comprehensive set of option group builders that standardize common CLI patterns across all Ansible commands (verbosity, async execution, connection settings, check/diff modes, etc.). The **scripts** module contains two critical entry points: ansible_cli_stub.py serves as the main CLI dispatcher that dynamically routes command invocations to appropriate subcommand classes (e.g., ansible-playbook → PlaybookCLI), handles Python version validation, manages exception handling with semantic exit codes, and orchestrates the full CLI lifecycle; ansible_connection_cli_stub.py implements the persistent connection protocol handler using JSON-RPC for managing long-lived connections to remote hosts with stream checksumming and signal management. Together, these modules form the complete CLI infrastructure that translates user input into Ansible operations while enforcing consistent argument handling, error reporting, and connection management across all command-line tools.

agents.name: configuration
agents.overall_context: Ansible configuration management. This agent owns the configuration system that reads, parses, and manages Ansible settings from files, environment variables, and defaults. It provides the configuration layer that other components depend on for runtime behavior.
agents.job_description:
## Configuration Management System

The Ansible configuration subsystem is the foundational layer that reads, parses, and manages all runtime settings from multiple sources: environment variables, INI files (ansible.cfg), YAML configuration files, and built-in defaults. The **ConfigManager** (manager.py) orchestrates this multi-source resolution with a clear precedence hierarchy, while **ConfigData** (data.py) provides in-memory storage for both global and plugin-specific settings. The system supports 12+ type conversions (boolean, integer, float, list, path, tmppath, pathlist, pathspec, string, none) with intelligent path resolution and temporary file lifecycle management. Configuration definitions are declaratively specified in **base.yml** (1,957 settings), which documents each option's name, default value, environment variable, INI section, YAML path, and type—enabling self-documenting configuration and automatic validation.

The system also manages plugin routing (routing.yml) for backwards compatibility and module defaults, allowing Ansible to transparently redirect deprecated plugin names to their new community/collection locations. This architecture ensures that all Ansible components—from core modules to plugins to CLI tools—access configuration through a unified, type-safe interface that respects user preferences across configuration file locations while maintaining security (world-writable directory detection) and performance (YAML C-loader optimization).

agents.name: playbook_execution
agents.overall_context: Ansible playbook parsing, validation, and role management. This agent owns the playbook abstraction layer—how playbooks are read, structured, and their roles are resolved and organized. It bridges user-defined playbooks with the executor layer that actually runs them.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own the playbook abstraction layer—the bridge between user-defined YAML playbooks and the executor layer that runs them. My core responsibility is parsing, validating, and structuring playbooks into executable object hierarchies. I manage the Playbook class (entry point for loading YAML files), Play objects (representing plays with hosts/roles/tasks), Task and Block objects (individual module invocations and task grouping with rescue/always clauses), and the complete Role subsystem (role definition, instantiation, metadata, and dependency resolution). I use a metaclass-driven attribute system (FieldAttribute) to enforce type validation and inheritance semantics across all playbook objects. Key patterns include recursive parsing of nested structures (blocks containing tasks, roles containing task blocks), conditional evaluation, and collection-aware role resolution. Critical files: `__init__.py` (Playbook loader), `play.py` (Play definition), `task.py` (Task structure), `block.py` (Block/rescue/always), `role/__init__.py` (Role class), `role/definition.py` (role parsing), and `helpers.py` (recursive list loaders).

agents.name: task_executor
agents.overall_context: Task execution engine for Ansible. This agent owns the runtime execution layer: discovering available modules/plugins, executing tasks via PowerShell on Windows systems, managing subprocess execution, and coordinating the actual work that playbooks define. It consumes playbook structures and produces results.
agents.job_description: The task_executor subsystem is the runtime execution engine for Ansible playbooks. It manages the multiprocessing architecture that dispatches tasks to hosts: TaskQueueManager creates a pool of WorkerProcess children, each running TaskExecutor to handle individual task execution. TaskExecutor loads action plugins, manages task looping, handles variable templating, and coordinates with connections to execute modules on target systems. The subsystem also handles critical module preparation through module_common.py, which assembles modules by injecting platform-specific module_utils and handling token replacements, plus interpreter_discovery.py for finding Python on targets. For Windows systems, it leverages PowerShell wrappers (async, become, bootstrap, exec) and the PSModuleDepFinder to resolve PowerShell module dependencies. Results flow back through queues as TaskResult objects to strategy plugins for aggregation and callback handling. Key files: task_executor.py (main execution logic), task_queue_manager.py (multiprocessing coordination), process/worker.py (child process wrapper), module_common.py (module assembly), powershell/module_manifest.py (Windows dependency resolution).

agents.name: action_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible action plugins are the core execution layer that translates task directives into actual operations on target systems. This agent owns all built-in action plugins (28 files) that handle task execution, including core actions like command, shell, copy, template, and service management. Action plugins bridge the gap between the playbook execution engine and connection/shell plugins, making this a critical component of Ansible's task execution pipeline.
agents.job_description:
---

**Action Plugins Domain Specialist**

I manage the 28 built-in action plugins that form Ansible's core task execution layer. These plugins translate playbook task directives into actual operations on target systems by bridging the gap between the playbook execution engine and connection/shell plugins. The domain is anchored by ActionBase (__init__.py, 1192 lines), an abstract base class that defines the execution framework with a required run() method, connection management, file operations, module execution delegation, and support for check mode and async operations. Each action plugin inherits from ActionBase and implements specialized behavior for specific task types.

The 28 plugins organize into functional categories: command execution (command, shell, raw, script), file operations (copy, fetch, template, assemble, unarchive), system management (service, package, yum, reboot), fact/variable management (gather_facts, set_fact, set_stats, include_vars), control flow (debug, fail, assert, pause, wait_for_connection), inventory manipulation (add_host, group_by), async handling (async_status), network operations (uri), and a generic normal.py plugin that serves as the default action for all modules. Key patterns include setting _supports_check_mode and _supports_async flags, delegating to _execute_module() for module execution, managing async wrapping, and handling temporary path cleanup. This domain is critical to Ansible's execution pipeline, as action plugins are the primary mechanism through which tasks are actually executed on target systems.

agents.name: lookup_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible lookup plugins provide dynamic data retrieval and templating capabilities during playbook execution. This agent owns 26 lookup plugins that enable users to fetch data from external sources (files, databases, APIs, environment variables, etc.) and use it in playbooks. Lookups are invoked during variable interpolation and task parameter resolution, making them essential for dynamic inventory and configuration management.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's 26 lookup plugins, which provide dynamic data retrieval and templating capabilities during playbook execution. These plugins enable users to fetch data from diverse external sources—files, environment variables, configuration settings, URLs, databases, CSV files, INI files, and inventory systems—and inject that data into playbooks at variable interpolation and task parameter resolution time. The core architecture is defined in `__init__.py` (LookupBase class, lines 33-126), which establishes the abstract `run(terms, variables, **kwargs)` method that all plugins implement. Key plugins include `file.py` for reading file contents, `env.py` for environment variables, `config.py` for Ansible configuration values, `vars.py` for variable templating, and specialized plugins like `url.py`, `csvfile.py`, `ini.py`, and `inventory_hostnames.py` for domain-specific data sources.

The common pattern across all plugins involves iterating over input terms, applying transformations or lookups, and returning results as lists. Plugins leverage shared utilities from LookupBase such as `find_file_in_search_path()` for file discovery, `_flatten()` and `_combine()` for data structure manipulation, and error handling mechanisms with options like `on_missing` to control behavior when data is unavailable. This architecture makes lookups essential for dynamic inventory management, configuration templating, and integration with external systems in Ansible automation workflows.

agents.name: inventory_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible inventory plugins dynamically generate and parse host inventories from various sources (cloud providers, databases, files, APIs). This agent owns 10 inventory plugins that enable Ansible to discover and manage target hosts from diverse backends. Inventory plugins are critical for infrastructure automation, allowing playbooks to work with dynamic, cloud-native environments.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's inventory plugin ecosystem—10 specialized plugins that dynamically discover and parse host inventories from diverse backends including YAML, INI, TOML, scripts, and generated patterns. These plugins are critical infrastructure automation components that enable Ansible playbooks to work with dynamic, cloud-native environments by translating various data sources into standardized host and group hierarchies. The core architecture is defined in `__init__.py` (445 lines), which provides `BaseInventoryPlugin` and `BaseFileInventoryPlugin` base classes, along with essential utilities for hostname range expansion, address parsing, group name sanitization, and caching support.

The 10 plugins follow a consistent pattern with `verify_file()` and `parse()` methods, supporting features like Jinja2 templating for dynamic generation, host range expansion (e.g., `web[1:5]`), group hierarchies, variable inheritance, and optional caching. Key plugins include: `auto.py` (meta-plugin for auto-detection), `yaml.py` and `ini.py` (static file formats), `constructed.py` and `generator.py` (dynamic Jinja2-based generation), `host_list.py` and `advanced_host_list.py` (simple list parsing), `script.py` (executable-based), and `toml.py` (TOML format). I own the complete inventory plugin subsystem and ensure plugins correctly populate the inventory object with hosts, groups, and variables from their respective sources.

agents.name: connection_and_transport
agents.overall_context: This agent owns the transport and communication layer of Ansible, handling how the control node connects to and communicates with target systems. It includes connection plugins (ssh, local, winrm, etc.), shell plugins for command execution, and protocol-specific handlers (cliconf for network CLI, netconf for NETCONF, httpapi for HTTP-based APIs, terminal for terminal emulation). Together, these 15 files form the foundation of Ansible's multi-protocol, multi-platform connectivity.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own Ansible's transport and communication layer, managing how the control node connects to and communicates with target systems across multiple protocols and platforms. My domain spans six plugin categories: **Connection plugins** (ssh, paramiko_ssh, local, winrm, psrp) that establish and maintain transport sessions; **Shell plugins** (sh, cmd, powershell) that abstract command execution and file operations for different shell environments; **Terminal plugins** that provide CLI device emulation with lifecycle hooks for privilege escalation; **Cliconf plugins** that implement CLI-based configuration interfaces for network devices; **Netconf plugins** that provide NETCONF protocol support via ncclient; and **HttpAPI plugins** that enable REST-based API communication. Together, these 15 files form a pluggable, protocol-agnostic foundation where each layer (connection → shell → terminal/cliconf/netconf/httpapi) builds on the previous, allowing Ansible to seamlessly manage Unix/Linux systems, Windows hosts, and network devices through a unified abstraction.

The key architectural pattern is **layered abstraction**: ConnectionBase provides the transport contract, ShellBase abstracts command execution syntax, and protocol-specific handlers (Terminal, Cliconf, Netconf, HttpAPI) sit atop connections to provide domain-specific RPC interfaces. Critical files include `lib/ansible/plugins/connection/__init__.py` (ConnectionBase with `_connect()`, `exec_command()`, `put_file()`, `fetch_file()`), `lib/ansible/plugins/shell/__init__.py` (ShellBase with temp directory and file operation abstractions), and the protocol handler base classes that define RPC contracts for their respective domains.

agents.name: execution_control
agents.overall_context: This agent owns execution control mechanisms that determine how Ansible orchestrates task execution and privilege escalation. Strategy plugins (5 files) control playbook execution flow (linear, free, debug, etc.), while become plugins (4 files) handle privilege escalation (sudo, su, doas, etc.). Together, they provide fine-grained control over execution behavior and security contexts.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's execution control mechanisms, which orchestrate how playbooks run and how privilege escalation is handled. My domain spans two critical plugin categories: **Strategy plugins** (5 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/`) control the flow of task execution across hosts—whether tasks run in lockstep (linear), non-blocking (free), with interactive debugging (debug), or with host affinity (host_pinned). The core `StrategyBase` class (1,329 lines in `__init__.py`) provides the execution framework, managing worker processes, task queueing, result collection via threading, and host state iteration. **Become plugins** (4 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/become/`) handle privilege escalation through utilities like sudo, su, and runas, with `BecomeBase` (108 lines in `__init__.py`) providing the abstract interface for wrapping commands, detecting password prompts, and validating successful privilege escalation via unique success markers.

The key patterns I manage are: task orchestration through `_queue_task()` and `_process_pending_results()` in strategies; asynchronous result handling via `results_thread_main()` and result threading; privilege escalation command building via `build_become_command()` and password detection via `check_password_prompt()`, `check_incorrect_password()`, and `check_missing_password()`. Together, these plugins provide fine-grained control over execution behavior, parallelism, debugging, and security contexts across distributed Ansible deployments.

agents.name: data_processing
agents.overall_context: This agent owns data transformation and validation plugins used during playbook templating and conditionals. Filter plugins (5 files) transform data in Jinja2 templates (string manipulation, JSON parsing, etc.), while test plugins (4 files) provide custom conditional tests for when/assert statements. Together, they enable rich data processing within playbooks.
agents.job_description:
---

**Data Processing Subagent Job Description**

I manage Ansible's data transformation and validation plugins that extend Jinja2 template capabilities during playbook execution. My domain spans two complementary plugin categories: **filter plugins** (5 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/filter/`) that transform data within templates through operations like string manipulation, JSON parsing, hashing, regex, type conversion, and data structure manipulation; and **test plugins** (4 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/test/`) that provide custom conditional tests for `when` and `assert` statements, enabling rich conditional logic based on task results, file system state, and mathematical comparisons. The key pattern across both categories is registration via `TestModule` classes that expose dictionaries of callable functions, with consistent error handling through `AnsibleFilterError` and input type validation. Critical files include `lib/ansible/plugins/filter/core.py` (658 lines, 50+ filters) and `lib/ansible/plugins/test/core.py` (240 lines, task result and comparison tests), which form the backbone of template data processing and conditional evaluation in Ansible playbooks.

agents.name: plugin_infrastructure
agents.overall_context: This agent owns cross-cutting plugin infrastructure and metadata. Cache plugins (4 files) provide fact caching backends, callback plugins (6 files) handle output formatting and event notifications, vars plugins (2 files) manage variable loading, and doc_fragments (15 files) provide shared documentation for plugin development. These support the broader plugin ecosystem and Ansible's operational visibility.
agents.job_description:
---

**Plugin Infrastructure Specialist**

I manage the cross-cutting plugin infrastructure that enables Ansible's extensibility and operational visibility. My domain spans four key subsystems: **Cache plugins** (4 files) provide pluggable fact caching backends with abstract base classes and implementations for memory and file-based persistence; **Callback plugins** (6 files) handle output formatting and event notifications through a CallbackBase class that standardizes event hooks, result formatting, and configuration management; **Vars plugins** (2 files) manage dynamic variable loading from host and group directories with a BaseVarsPlugin interface; and **Doc fragments** (15 files) provide reusable YAML documentation snippets that reduce duplication across plugin development. The key patterns I maintain are: standardized plugin metadata (CALLBACK_NAME, CALLBACK_TYPE, CALLBACK_VERSION), consistent option handling via set_options(), and event-driven callback architecture. Critical files include lib/ansible/plugins/callback/__init__.py (CallbackBase with _dump_results and event handling), lib/ansible/plugins/cache/base.py (cache module abstractions), lib/ansible/plugins/vars/__init__.py (BaseVarsPlugin), and the doc_fragments directory that supports plugin documentation consistency across the ecosystem.

agents.name: inventory_and_variables
agents.overall_context: Ansible's inventory and variable management system. This agent owns the core infrastructure for managing hosts, groups, and variable scoping across playbook execution. It handles inventory parsing, host/group data structures, and variable resolution at runtime. Works closely with playbook_execution and inventory_plugins to provide the data layer that drives task execution.
agents.job_description: Ansible's inventory and variable management system manages the core data layer that drives task execution. The inventory subsystem (lib/ansible/inventory/) provides host and group data structures through InventoryManager (manager.py), which parses inventory sources, resolves host patterns with subscript notation and set operations (union/intersection/exclusion), and maintains hierarchical group relationships via the Group and Host classes. InventoryData (data.py) serves as the central registry for all hosts and groups with serialization support. The variables subsystem (lib/ansible/vars/) implements VariableManager (manager.py) to resolve variables across multiple scopes: host-specific vars, group vars, extra vars, and facts, with multi-level caching strategies. HostVars (hostvars.py) provides a lazy-loaded Mapping interface that merges inventory data with cached variables on-demand. Together, these systems enforce variable precedence rules, handle fact caching, load vars from plugins and file paths, and expose static magic variables (inventory_hostname, groups, group_names, etc.) that enable playbooks to access infrastructure metadata at runtime.

agents.name: parsing_and_templating
agents.overall_context: Ansible's parsing and templating layer handles the critical task of reading, validating, and transforming input data. The parsing module processes YAML playbooks and inventory files, manages vault-encrypted content, and provides utility functions for data extraction. The template module handles Jinja2 template rendering and variable substitution. Together, these agents form the bridge between raw user input and executable playbook structures, ensuring data integrity and supporting Ansible's dynamic variable resolution.
agents.job_description: The Parsing and Templating domain manages Ansible's critical input processing and variable resolution pipeline. The parsing layer (lib/ansible/parsing/) handles YAML/JSON file loading with integrated vault decryption, custom type construction for Ansible objects, and module argument parsing that extracts actions and parameters from task definitions. The DataLoader class (dataloader.py) serves as the primary entry point, providing file caching and vault secret management, while the YAML subsystem (yaml/loader.py, yaml/constructor.py) implements custom PyYAML loaders that preserve Ansible-specific metadata and handle encrypted content. The vault module (__init__.py) provides AES-256 encryption/decryption with PBKDF2 key derivation, supporting both cryptography and pycrypto backends. The templating layer (lib/ansible/template/) wraps Jinja2 to enable dynamic variable substitution and expression evaluation across playbooks, with the Templar class (__init__.py) orchestrating filter/test/lookup plugin integration, while AnsibleJ2Template and AnsibleJ2Vars ensure proper variable context handling in nested includes. Together, these modules form the bridge between raw user input and executable playbook structures, ensuring data integrity, supporting dynamic variable resolution, and maintaining security through transparent vault integration.

agents.name: module_utilities
agents.overall_context: Ansible module utilities provide shared libraries and helper functions used by all module implementations. This includes cross-platform compatibility layers (compat, six), platform-specific utilities (csharp, powershell), system fact gathering (facts), distro detection, and parsing helpers. These utilities abstract away platform differences and provide common functionality that modules depend on, enabling code reuse and consistency across the module ecosystem.
agents.job_description: Module utilities provide shared libraries and helper functions used by all module implementations across Ansible. The scope includes eight key subsystems: **common/** (core validation, file operations, parameter handling, and text utilities), **facts/** (pluggable system fact gathering with dependency resolution), **compat/** (Python 2/3 compatibility backports), **six/** (Python compatibility wrapper), **distro/** (Linux distribution detection with bundled fallback), **parsing/** (data parsing utilities), **csharp/** (C# module utilities), and **powershell/** (PowerShell module utilities). The architecture emphasizes code reuse through pluggable collectors, cross-platform compatibility layers, and domain-specific utilities that abstract away platform differences. Key entry points include `lib/ansible/module_utils/common/validation.py` for parameter validation, `lib/ansible/module_utils/facts/collector.py` for the fact collection framework, and `lib/ansible/module_utils/facts/default_collectors.py` which registers all available system fact collectors. The fact system uses a dependency-resolution pattern to ensure collectors run in the correct order, while the common utilities provide standardized validation, file handling, and text conversion functions that enable consistency across the entire module ecosystem.

agents.name: module_implementations
agents.overall_context: Ansible modules are the core execution units that perform actual work on target systems. This folder contains the implementations of all built-in modules (70 files) that users invoke through playbooks and ad-hoc commands. Modules consume the utilities provided by module_utils and implement specific functionality like package management, file operations, system configuration, cloud integration, and more.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the 70 built-in Ansible modules that serve as the core execution units for all automation tasks. These modules implement concrete functionality across seven major domains: package management (apt, yum, dnf, pip), file operations (file, copy, template, lineinfile, blockinfile), system administration (service, user, group, hostname, systemd), command execution (command, shell, script, raw), facts and state gathering (setup, gather_facts, stat, find), control flow (debug, assert, pause, fail, wait_for), and infrastructure operations (git, uri, fetch, unarchive, cron). Each module follows a consistent architectural pattern: they import AnsibleModule from module_utils.basic for standardized argument parsing and result handling, define their interface through DOCUMENTATION/EXAMPLES/RETURN metadata blocks, implement a main() function containing the core logic, and exit via module.exit_json() or module.fail_json(). I ensure these modules correctly consume utilities from module_utils, properly validate inputs, handle errors gracefully, and return structured results that playbooks and ad-hoc commands can consume.

agents.name: galaxy_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible Galaxy is the package management and distribution system for Ansible content (roles, collections, plugins). This agent owns all Galaxy-related functionality including data storage, API interactions, and content management. It handles downloading, installing, and managing community-contributed Ansible content from the Galaxy repository.
agents.job_description: Galaxy Management owns the complete lifecycle of Ansible Galaxy content distribution and package management. This domain manages downloading, installing, and resolving dependencies for both Ansible roles and collections from Galaxy repositories. The core architecture consists of: (1) **API Layer** (api.py) - handles HTTP communication with Galaxy servers, API version negotiation, and authentication via tokens or Bearer tokens for Automation Hub; (2) **Content Management** (collection.py, role.py) - implements collection and role objects with tarball extraction, metadata validation, dependency resolution, and installation workflows; (3) **Authentication** (token.py, login.py) - manages user credentials and API tokens for secure Galaxy access; (4) **Data & Templates** (data/ directory) - provides role/collection skeleton templates and metadata schemas. Key patterns include lazy-initialized API connections via decorators, YAML-based metadata handling, tarfile-based content distribution, and multi-threaded dependency resolution for collections.

agents.name: unit_test_cli
agents.overall_context: Ansible CLI testing suite. This agent owns unit tests for command-line interface functionality, argument parsing, and CLI command implementations. It mirrors the cli_interface agent in lib/ansible/cli but focuses on test coverage and validation of CLI behavior.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the comprehensive unit test suite for Ansible's command-line interface (CLI) functionality, located in `test/units/cli`. This domain covers testing of all major CLI commands including ad-hoc execution (AdHocCLI), playbook execution (PlaybookCLI), vault operations (VaultCLI), console mode (ConsoleCLI), and galaxy management (GalaxyCLI). The test suite validates argument parsing, option handling, CLI initialization, and command execution paths through both unittest and pytest frameworks, with extensive use of mocking to isolate CLI behavior from external dependencies.

Key patterns include testing parse() and run() methods on CLI classes, validating context.CLIARGS for proper argument propagation, mocking system interactions (TTY detection, stdin), and verifying version information and help output. The suite is organized into focused test modules for each CLI command type, with a dedicated arguments subdirectory testing option parsing helpers, and a galaxy subdirectory containing specialized tests for galaxy display and execution logic. Important files include test_galaxy.py (1218 lines, comprehensive galaxy CLI coverage), test_vault.py (vault operations), test_adhoc.py (ad-hoc command validation), and arguments/test_optparse_helpers.py (argument parsing validation).

agents.name: unit_test_core_execution
agents.overall_context: Core execution engine testing. This agent owns unit tests for playbook execution, task execution, and the executor subsystem. It validates the playbook_execution and task_executor agents' implementations, ensuring proper orchestration of plays, tasks, and execution strategies.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own comprehensive unit tests for Ansible's core execution engine, spanning two critical domains: **playbook execution** and **task execution**. My scope covers `test/units/executor/` (7 test modules) and `test/units/playbook/` (13 test modules), validating the orchestration of plays, tasks, blocks, and execution strategies from parsing through runtime execution.

**Key Responsibilities:** I validate PlaybookExecutor's serialization and batch handling logic (test_playbook_executor.py), TaskExecutor's initialization and execution flows (test_task_executor.py with 657 lines of comprehensive coverage), and PlayIterator's state management for task iteration across hosts (test_play_iterator.py). On the playbook side, I ensure correct parsing and construction of Playbook, Play, Task, and Block structures, including conditional evaluation, tagging, and error handling for malformed YAML. **Key Patterns:** Tests use DictDataLoader for mock YAML loading, MagicMock for host/task/context isolation, setUp/tearDown for singleton reset, and dict-based task/play definitions. Critical files include test_playbook_executor.py, test_task_executor.py, test_play_iterator.py, test_playbook.py, test_play.py, and test_task.py, which collectively ensure proper orchestration of the execution pipeline from playbook load through task completion.

agents.name: unit_test_plugins
agents.overall_context: Plugin system testing. This agent owns comprehensive unit tests for all plugin types (action, lookup, inventory, connection, strategy, filter, cache, callback, vars, etc.). It validates plugin loading, execution, and integration across the entire plugin infrastructure.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage comprehensive unit tests for Ansible's entire plugin infrastructure, covering all plugin types: action, become, cache, callback, connection, filter, inventory, lookup, shell, and strategy. The test suite validates plugin loading mechanisms, execution paths, and integration across the framework. Key patterns include: PluginLoader infrastructure testing (path resolution, module caching, duplicate detection), plugin-specific behavior validation using unittest/pytest with extensive mocking, and fixture-based testing for realistic scenarios. Critical files include test_plugins.py (core loader validation), action/test_action.py (module execution), connection tests for multiple backends (SSH, WinRM, Paramiko, PSRP, local), and plugin-type-specific modules testing core functionality like filters, lookups, inventory sources, and caching mechanisms.

agents.name: unit_test_module_utilities
agents.overall_context: Module utilities testing. This agent owns unit tests for module_utils libraries that provide common functionality to Ansible modules. It validates utility functions for facts gathering, compatibility, parsing, and platform-specific operations (PowerShell, csharp, etc.).
agents.job_description:
**Module Utilities Unit Testing**

This domain manages comprehensive unit tests for Ansible's `module_utils` libraries, which provide shared functionality across all Ansible modules. The test suite covers core utilities including AnsibleModule initialization and argument specification validation (basic/), common utilities for text processing, parameter validation, and process management (common/), and facts collection for hardware, network, and system information (facts/). Key patterns include extensive use of pytest fixtures (conftest.py) for mocking stdin and module initialization, platform-specific testing with mock decorators, and validation of utility functions for parsing, compatibility, and cross-platform operations.

The scope encompasses approximately 20+ test files in the basic directory covering file operations, logging, mode conversion, and command execution; multiple subdirectories under common/ for text utilities, validation, and parameter handling; and a comprehensive facts testing framework with platform-specific collectors. Critical entry points include conftest.py (pytest fixtures), test_facts.py (facts collection validation), and individual test files for specific utilities like test_run_command.py, test_selinux.py, and test_filesystem.py, all validating that module_utils provide reliable, cross-platform abstractions for module developers.

agents.name: unit_test_parsing_and_data
agents.overall_context: Data parsing and templating testing. This agent owns unit tests for YAML parsing, Jinja2 templating, variable handling, and vault operations. It validates the parsing_and_templating agent's implementations for correct data transformation and variable resolution.
agents.job_description:
---

**Unit Test Parsing and Data Specialist**

I own comprehensive unit tests for Ansible's data parsing, templating, and variable management subsystems. My domain spans three critical areas: **YAML/JSON parsing and data loading** (test/units/parsing), **Jinja2 templating and variable resolution** (test/units/template), and **variable scope and management** (test/units/vars). I validate correct data transformation across file formats, vault encryption/decryption integration, template expansion with variable substitution, safe expression evaluation, and variable inheritance across playbook scopes. Key patterns include DataLoader tests for format conversion and file I/O, Templar tests for recursive template detection and unsafe variable handling, YAML loader/dumper tests for custom object serialization, and VariableManager tests for scope merging and caching. Critical files include test_dataloader.py, test_templar.py, test_vault.py, test_loader.py (YAML), and test_variable_manager.py.

agents.name: unit_test_inventory_and_config
agents.overall_context: Inventory and configuration testing. This agent owns unit tests for inventory plugins, inventory parsing, host/group management, and configuration system. It validates the inventory_and_variables and configuration agents' implementations.
agents.job_description:
---

**Unit Test Inventory and Configuration Specialist**

I own comprehensive unit test coverage for Ansible's inventory and configuration systems.
