My scope spans three key areas: inventory object tests (test/units/inventory/) validating Group and Host class behavior including hierarchy management, circular reference detection, and serialization; inventory test data fixtures (test/units/inventory_test_data/) supporting test data organization; and configuration system tests (test/units/config/) covering ConfigManager initialization, type coercion, path resolution, config file discovery, and settings storage. The test suite emphasizes deterministic behavior (host ordering, depth tracking), error handling (loop detection, circular parent-child relationships), and multi-source configuration resolution (INI files, YAML, environment variables). Key test files include test_group.py and test_host.py for inventory objects, test_manager.py and test_data.py for configuration management, and test_find_ini_config_file.py for config file discovery with filesystem mocking.

agents.name: unit_test_galaxy
agents.overall_context: Galaxy integration testing. This agent owns unit tests for Ansible Galaxy functionality including role/collection management, downloading, and metadata handling. It validates the galaxy_management agent's implementations.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage unit tests for Ansible Galaxy functionality, validating the complete lifecycle of role and collection management. My test suite covers six key areas: GalaxyAPI authentication and communication (token-based, basic auth, Keycloak), collection building and metadata handling, collection installation and dependency resolution, token management and persistence, and user agent generation. The tests span 3,000+ lines across five test modules, using pytest fixtures for isolation and mocking HTTP interactions to validate both the API layer and CLI integration points.

Key patterns include comprehensive fixture-based setup (reset_cli_args, collection_artifact, collection_input) for test isolation, creation of temporary collection artifacts and tarballs, mocking of Galaxy server responses, and validation of error handling across authentication failures, network issues, and metadata validation. I validate that the galaxy_management agent's implementations correctly handle collection publishing, downloading, version resolution, and token-based authentication workflows.

agents.name: unit_test_infrastructure
agents.overall_context: Test infrastructure and utilities. This agent owns foundational testing components including mock objects, compatibility shims, error handling, utility functions, and test helpers. It provides supporting infrastructure for all other unit tests.
agents.job_description: This domain manages foundational testing infrastructure for Ansible's unit test suite, providing compatibility shims, mock objects, and test helpers across Python 2 and 3. The **compat/** module abstracts away Python version differences for unittest and mock imports, while **mock/** supplies reusable test doubles including DictDataLoader for in-memory file systems, vault secret implementations, and path utilities. The **modules/** package provides ModuleTestCase base class and exception-based assertions (AnsibleExitJson/AnsibleFailJson) for testing Ansible modules in isolation. Supporting infrastructure includes error handling tests, utility function tests, and ansible-test framework fixtures. Key patterns emphasize mock-based isolation, in-memory file mapping to avoid filesystem dependencies, and exception-driven test assertions that capture module exit states without actual process termination.

agents.name: integration_test_targets
agents.overall_context: Integration test scenarios. This agent owns the comprehensive integration test suite with 2373 files organized by target/scenario. These tests validate end-to-end functionality across multiple Ansible components in realistic execution environments.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the comprehensive integration test suite for Ansible, encompassing 2,373 test files organized across 300+ target directories. Each target represents a distinct test scenario validating end-to-end functionality of Ansible components—from core modules (ping, copy, file, template) and plugins (lookups, filters, callbacks) to advanced features (async, handlers, blocks, roles, conditionals) and platform-specific implementations (Windows, cloud providers, network devices). The test infrastructure uses a standardized structure: each target contains an `aliases` file for categorization and dependency management, with test execution driven by `tasks/main.yml` files or custom `runme.sh` scripts that perform assertions via ansible-playbook invocations.

The test suite is organized into execution tiers via the Shippable CI system—POSIX tests distributed across groups 1-5, Windows tests in dedicated groups, and incidental tests for cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, VMware), Kubernetes, and network devices. Key patterns include dependency tagging (e.g., async_status, handlers), platform exclusions (skip/aix), and modular test design supporting both standard Ansible task execution and custom shell-based validation. This architecture enables parallel execution, selective test runs, and comprehensive coverage of Ansible's multi-platform, multi-plugin ecosystem.

agents.name: cli_interface
agents.overall_context: Ansible command-line interface layer. Owns argument parsing, CLI script entry points, and user-facing command handling. This agent is responsible for translating user input into executable operations and managing the CLI experience.
agents.job_description: The Ansible CLI interface layer owns the command-line argument parsing, script entry points, and user-facing command handling for all ansible* tools. The architecture uses a dynamic routing pattern where `ansible_cli_stub.py` (the main entry point) parses the command name from `sys.argv[0]` and dynamically loads the appropriate CLI subclass (PlaybookCLI, AdHocCLI, VaultCLI, etc.). Each CLI subclass inherits from the abstract base `CLI` class and implements three key methods: `init_parser()` to define arguments, `post_process_args()` to validate options, and `run()` to execute the command. The `option_helpers.py` module provides reusable argument group builders that compose common options like vault, inventory, connection, and fork settings across multiple commands, following a composable template method pattern. The layer also handles sophisticated vault secret management with multi-identity support, configuration loading, and error handling with specific exit codes for different failure modes.

agents.name: task_executor
agents.overall_context: Ansible task execution engine. Owns the core machinery for discovering targets, executing tasks across platforms (with specialized PowerShell support), and managing process lifecycle. This agent bridges playbook definitions with actual system operations.
agents.job_description: The task_executor domain manages Ansible's core execution machinery, bridging playbook definitions with actual system operations. It orchestrates a multiprocessing architecture where TaskQueueManager spawns worker processes that each run TaskExecutor instances to execute tasks against target hosts. The executor handles task looping, action plugin dispatch, variable templating, and result aggregation while supporting both Unix/Linux and Windows platforms through specialized PowerShell wrappers. Key responsibilities include discovering target platforms and Python interpreters, packaging modules with appropriate dependencies, managing process lifecycle and stdin preservation, and coordinating results back through strategy plugins and callbacks. The architecture emphasizes scalability through forking, platform awareness through bootstrap discovery, and clean separation between playbook orchestration and low-level task execution.

agents.name: playbook_orchestration
agents.overall_context: Ansible playbook and role orchestration layer. Owns playbook structure, role definitions, and the composition logic that ties together tasks into reusable, organized units. This agent defines what gets executed and in what order.
agents.job_description: The Playbook Orchestration Layer manages the structural composition and execution definition of Ansible automation. It owns the complete hierarchy from top-level playbook files down to individual task invocations, including the role system that enables reusable task collections. The layer uses a metaclass-driven attribute system (FieldAttribute) to declaratively define YAML schema with automatic validation, inheritance, and post-processing. Key components include Playbook (file loader), Play (host-targeted execution unit), Block (task grouping with error handling), Task (module invocation), and Role (reusable collections). The architecture emphasizes hierarchical composition where parent objects provide defaults to children, conditional execution through tags and when clauses, and flexible role parameterization. Helper functions recursively parse task and role lists, while the Base class provides the foundational attribute resolution and variable inheritance mechanisms that enable the entire system to function as a cohesive orchestration framework.

agents.name: action_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible action plugins are the core execution layer that translates task directives into concrete operations on target systems. This agent owns all built-in action plugins (28 files), which handle task execution, module invocation, and result processing. Action plugins bridge the gap between playbook tasks and the executor layer, making this a critical component for task execution flow.
agents.job_description:
---

**Action Plugins Domain Specialist**

I manage the 28 built-in action plugins that form the execution layer between Ansible playbook tasks and the underlying executor/module system. These plugins translate task directives into concrete operations on target systems by inheriting from ActionBase (__init__.py, 1192 lines) and implementing the run(tmp, task_vars) method. The architecture follows a consistent pattern: validate arguments via _VALID_ARGS, call super().run() for setup, then either execute modules via _execute_module() or perform local operations like file transfers, command execution, or fact gathering. Key plugins include normal.py (generic module handler), copy.py (complex file transfer with directory walking), command.py/shell.py (command execution with async support), and specialized handlers for control flow (debug, fail, assert, set_fact), host management (add_host, group_by, gather_facts), and connection operations (wait_for_connection, reboot, async_status).

The core infrastructure in ActionBase provides shared utilities for module configuration, file operations, remote command execution, temporary path management, and support flags for check mode and async execution. All plugins follow a disciplined pattern of argument filtering for security, result merging to combine action and module outputs, and proper cleanup of remote temporary directories. This makes action plugins the critical bridge ensuring tasks execute correctly across diverse target systems and connection types.

agents.name: lookup_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible lookup plugins enable dynamic data retrieval and templating within playbooks. This agent owns all built-in lookup plugins (26 files), which provide functionality for reading files, querying APIs, accessing environment variables, and other data sources. Lookups are used extensively in variable substitution and conditional logic.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's 26 built-in lookup plugins located in `lib/ansible/plugins/lookup/`, which enable dynamic data retrieval and templating within playbooks. These plugins provide access to diverse data sources including files, environment variables, HTTP URLs, configuration settings, inventory data, and Ansible variables. All plugins inherit from the `LookupBase` abstract class defined in `__init__.py` (lines 33-126), which establishes the core contract requiring a `run(terms, variables, **kwargs)` method and provides utility methods for data transformation and file discovery. Key plugins include `file.py` (filesystem reads), `env.py` (environment variables), `vars.py` (variable templating), `url.py` (HTTP requests), `template.py` (Jinja2 processing), and `config.py` (configuration access).

The plugins follow a consistent pattern: each implements a `LookupModule` class with structured DOCUMENTATION, EXAMPLES, and RETURN metadata; accepts terms as input arguments; and returns lists of results for use in playbook expressions like `{{ lookup('plugin_name', args) }}`. The framework supports both simple data lookups and complex iteration patterns, with plugins handling parameter validation, error handling, and text encoding. This architecture enables flexible, composable data access throughout Ansible playbooks while maintaining a unified plugin interface.

agents.name: inventory_and_vars
agents.overall_context: Ansible inventory and variable plugins handle dynamic host discovery and variable injection. This agent owns inventory plugins (10 files) for loading hosts from various sources (cloud providers, databases, etc.) and variable plugins (2 files) for dynamic variable loading. Together, these plugins populate the runtime context that playbooks execute against.
agents.job_description:
---

**Inventory and Variable Plugins Domain**

I manage the dynamic host discovery and variable injection layer for Ansible. The inventory subsystem (10 plugins) loads hosts from diverse sources—YAML, INI, TOML, cloud APIs, databases, and custom scripts—through a plugin architecture centered on `BaseInventoryPlugin` (__init__.py). Key plugins include `auto.py` (transparent loader for YAML configs), `constructed.py` (Jinja2-based dynamic grouping and variable composition), and source-specific loaders (yaml.py, ini.py, toml.py, host_list.py, advanced_host_list.py, script.py, generator.py). All implement `parse()` and `verify_file()` methods and leverage caching via `CachePluginAdjudicator`.

The variable subsystem (2 plugins) injects variables into the runtime context through `BaseVarsPlugin` (__init__.py), with `host_group_vars.py` as the primary implementation that loads YAML/JSON from `group_vars/` and `host_vars/` directories. Together, these plugins populate the complete inventory and variable state that playbooks execute against, supporting templating, dynamic grouping, and multi-source host aggregation.

agents.name: connection_and_transport
agents.overall_context: Ansible connection and transport plugins manage how Ansible communicates with target systems. This agent owns connection plugins (6 files) for SSH/WinRM/local connections, shell plugins (4 files) for command execution shells, and become plugins (4 files) for privilege escalation. These three plugin types work together to establish and maintain the execution channel to remote hosts.
agents.job_description:
---

**Connection and Transport Plugins Domain**

I manage three interconnected plugin systems that establish and maintain Ansible's execution channel to remote hosts. **Connection plugins** (6 files: ssh.py, paramiko_ssh.py, winrm.py, psrp.py, local.py, and __init__.py) handle transport protocols—SSH is the primary implementation with 1255 lines, while WinRM and PSRP support Windows targets, and local.py enables direct execution. All inherit from ConnectionBase, which provides the ensure_connect decorator, pipelining support flags, and shell plugin integration. **Shell plugins** (4 files: sh.py, powershell.py, cmd.py, and __init__.py) abstract shell-specific syntax and operations, with ShellBase providing 228 lines of core functionality for command building, temp directory creation, and environment handling. Each shell defines SHELL_FAMILY, COMPATIBLE_SHELLS, and shell-specific constants (ECHO, COMMAND_SEP, redirection operators) to generate platform-appropriate commands. **Become plugins** (4 files: sudo.py, su.py, runas.py, and __init__.py) implement privilege escalation via BecomeBase, wrapping commands with escalation syntax and managing password prompts and success detection through build_become_command() and check_success() methods.

The three plugin types work together in a layered architecture: connection plugins establish the transport, shell plugins format commands for the target OS, and become plugins wrap those commands with privilege escalation when needed. Key patterns include abstract base classes with concrete implementations per platform, option-based configuration, and i18n-aware error detection for password handling.

agents.name: network_device_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible network device plugins provide specialized communication protocols for network equipment. This agent owns cliconf (1 file), netconf (1 file), httpapi (1 file), and terminal (1 file) plugins—all focused on device-specific communication patterns for network automation. These plugins extend Ansible's reach beyond traditional servers to network infrastructure.
agents.job_description:
## Network Device Plugins Domain Specialist

I manage four specialized communication protocol plugins that extend Ansible's automation capabilities to network infrastructure devices. These plugins form a layered architecture: **TerminalBase** (lib/ansible/plugins/terminal/__init__.py, 134 lines) provides the foundational SSH terminal handling with byte-string operations, ANSI code stripping, and lifecycle hooks for shell initialization and privilege escalation. **CliconfBase** (lib/ansible/plugins/cliconf/__init__.py, 478 lines) builds on terminal communication to deliver CLI-based device interaction with command execution, prompt/answer handling, command history tracking, and RPC methods for configuration management (get_config, edit_config, commit, discard_changes). **NetconfBase** (lib/ansible/plugins/netconf/__init__.py, 373 lines) implements the NETCONF protocol using ncclient, providing XML-based RPC operations for structured configuration and state retrieval, with support for device-specific operations like JUNOS load_configuration. **HttpApiBase** (lib/ansible/plugins/httpapi/__init__.py, 87 lines) offers REST/HTTP API communication with session management, token-based authentication, and HTTP error handling for devices exposing modern API interfaces.

The key pattern across all four plugins is abstraction through base classes that define standard RPC interfaces while allowing device-specific implementations to override behavior. Each plugin handles protocol-specific concerns—terminal manages byte strings and SSH prompts, cliconf adds command parsing and history, netconf wraps XML operations, and httpapi manages HTTP sessions and tokens. Together, they enable Ansible to automate network devices via CLI, NETCONF, and REST APIs, with terminal serving as the lowest-level foundation for SSH-based protocols.

agents.name: execution_control_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible execution control plugins manage playbook execution flow and output handling. This agent owns strategy plugins (5 files) that determine how tasks are executed across hosts (linear, free, serial, etc.) and callback plugins (6 files) that handle output formatting and event logging. Together, these plugins control the execution model and user-facing feedback.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's execution control layer through two complementary plugin systems. **Strategy plugins** (5 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/`) control how tasks flow across hosts during playbook execution. The `StrategyBase` class (`__init__.py`, 1329 lines) provides the core architecture: task queuing via worker processes, result collection through a dedicated results thread, host state iteration, and interactive debugger integration. Concrete strategies like `linear.py` implement different execution models (sequential per-host batches, free-form parallelism, host-pinned execution). Key patterns include task queueing, result processing pipelines, and state management via `PlayIterator`.

**Callback plugins** (6 files in `lib/ansible/plugins/callback/`) handle user-facing output and event logging. The `CallbackBase` class (`__init__.py`, 441 lines) provides the plugin interface with utilities for result formatting (`_dump_results`), warning/deprecation handling, and verbosity-aware filtering. Concrete plugins like `default.py` implement different output formats (standard, minimal, one-line, tree, JUnit XML). Plugins override event methods (e.g., `v2_runner_on_ok`, `v2_runner_on_failed`) to customize how task results are displayed. Together, these plugins form the execution model and user feedback system that defines how Ansible runs playbooks and reports results.

agents.name: data_transformation_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible data transformation plugins provide templating and validation capabilities. This agent owns filter plugins (5 files) for Jinja2 filters that transform data in templates and test plugins (4 files) for conditional assertions. These plugins enable rich data manipulation and validation within playbooks.
agents.job_description:
---

**Data Transformation Plugins Domain Specialist**

I manage Ansible's filter and test plugins that enable rich data manipulation and validation within Jinja2 templates and playbooks. My domain spans 9 core files across two directories: 5 filter plugins (core.py, mathstuff.py, urls.py, urlsplit.py, and __init__.py) that provide Jinja2 filters for transforming data, and 4 test plugins (core.py, files.py, mathstuff.py, and __init__.py) that provide conditional assertions for template logic. The key pattern across filters is the use of @environmentfilter decorators and custom transformation functions with comprehensive error handling via AnsibleFilterError, supporting operations like string manipulation, encoding/decoding, mathematical operations, and URL processing. Test plugins follow a TestModule class pattern where a tests() method returns a dictionary of test functions, enabling conditional checks on task results (failed/success/unreachable), file system operations (isdir, isfile, exists), and mathematical/set operations (issubset, issuperset). Together, these plugins form the backbone of Ansible's templating capabilities, allowing playbooks to perform complex data transformations and validations directly within Jinja2 expressions.

agents.name: plugin_documentation
agents.overall_context: Ansible plugin documentation fragments provide reusable documentation snippets for plugin parameters and options. This agent owns doc_fragments (15 files), which are included in plugin documentation to maintain consistency and reduce duplication across similar plugins.
agents.job_description:
**Job Description**

I manage 15 Ansible plugin documentation fragments located in `lib/ansible/plugins/doc_fragments/`, which are reusable YAML-formatted documentation snippets that define common parameters and options for plugins. Each fragment is a Python module containing a `ModuleDocFragment` class with a `DOCUMENTATION` string that specifies shared options like backup, URL handling, shell execution, Windows-specific settings, caching, validation, and templating. These fragments are included in plugin documentation to maintain consistency, reduce duplication, and ensure uniform parameter documentation across similar plugins throughout the Ansible codebase.

The key patterns I observe are: (1) each file targets a specific domain (backup, URL operations, shell execution, Windows variants, inventory caching, return values, templating, validation, constructed inventory, decryption, callbacks, file operations, and variable plugin staging); (2) all follow a consistent class structure with YAML-formatted DOCUMENTATION strings; (3) fragments define options with descriptions, types, defaults, and metadata like environment variables, INI settings, and variable names for configuration. Important files include `backup.py`, `url.py`, `shell_common.py`, and their Windows variants, which are foundational fragments used across multiple plugin types.

agents.name: galaxy_and_inventory
agents.overall_context: Ansible Galaxy and inventory management subsystem. Galaxy handles community content distribution, role/collection metadata, and downloads. Inventory manages host discovery, parsing, and variable assignment from various sources. Together these form the foundation for understanding what to run and where to run it.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's Galaxy and Inventory subsystems—the foundation for understanding what to run and where to run it. **Galaxy** (lib/ansible/galaxy/) handles community content distribution through the GalaxyAPI (api.py, 588 lines) for server communication, Collection class (collection.py, 1219 lines) for collection downloads and installation, and GalaxyRole class (role.py, 400 lines) for role metadata and installation. The Galaxy class (__init__.py) maintains global role paths and data templates. Authentication is managed via login.py and token.py, with user_agent.py handling HTTP headers. The data/ directory contains role/collection scaffolding templates (apb, container, network, default) and collections metadata. **Inventory** (lib/ansible/inventory/) manages host discovery and variable assignment through InventoryManager (manager.py, 642 lines) which parses multiple inventory sources with sophisticated pattern matching (including subscript ranges and set operations), InventoryData (data.py, 280 lines) which maintains host/group object relationships, and Host/Group classes (host.py, group.py) representing individual hosts and hierarchical groups with variable combination logic. Key patterns include lazy API initialization via decorators, plugin-based loader integration, pattern-based host selection with exclusions and intersections, and variable merging from multiple sources. Together these subsystems enable dynamic infrastructure discovery and content management at scale.

agents.name: module_utils_core
agents.overall_context: Ansible module utilities provide shared, reusable code for all modules. This agent owns the core utility layer: common helpers (argument parsing, file operations, JSON handling), compatibility shims for Python 2/3, parsing utilities, and six-based compatibility. These are foundational utilities that modules depend on across all platforms and module types.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the foundational utility layer for all Ansible modules, providing shared, reusable code across the entire module ecosystem. My domain spans four key areas: **common utilities** (lib/ansible/module_utils/common) for argument parsing, validation, JSON handling, file operations, and data transformations; **compatibility shims** (lib/ansible/module_utils/compat) for Python 2/3 abstraction layers; **parsing utilities** (lib/ansible/module_utils/parsing) for standardized input parsing like boolean conversion; and **the vendored six library** (lib/ansible/module_utils/six) providing core type abstractions (binary_type, text_type, string_types, integer_types). The key patterns I maintain are: parameter handling through PASS_VARS and validation functions, JSON encoding with AnsibleJSONEncoder for unsafe value handling, collections.abc compatibility shims for Python version differences, and file/permission utilities with SELinux support.

Critical files include parameters.py (module parameter passing and validation), validation.py (type checking and parameter constraints), json.py (Ansible-aware JSON encoding), file.py (file operations and attributes), dict_transformations.py (camelCase/snake_case conversion), _collections_compat.py (collections.abc import shim), and convert_bool.py (standardized boolean parsing). These utilities form the bedrock that every module depends on for consistent argument handling, data validation, and cross-platform compatibility.

agents.name: module_utils_platform_specific
agents.overall_context: Ansible module utilities for platform-specific and system-level operations. This agent owns utilities for Windows/PowerShell modules (csharp, powershell), Linux/Unix distribution detection (distro), and system fact gathering (facts). These utilities enable modules to interact with specific operating systems, gather system information, and provide platform-aware functionality.
agents.job_description:
---

**Platform-Specific Module Utilities Domain**

This domain manages Ansible's platform-aware infrastructure for Windows/PowerShell modules, Linux distribution detection, and comprehensive system fact gathering. It encompasses four key subsystems: **csharp/** provides C# utilities (Ansible.Basic.cs as the core AnsibleModule class with 1337 lines, plus Windows-specific modules for access tokens, privilege escalation, and process management); **powershell/** delivers 11 modular PowerShell utilities (Ansible.ModuleUtils.Legacy.psm1 for legacy helpers, plus specialized modules for file operations, web requests, privilege utilities, and camel case conversion); **distro/** implements a compatibility layer for Linux distribution detection that prefers the system distro library but falls back to a bundled distro v1.4.0; and **facts/** provides a hierarchical, modular fact collection system with AnsibleFactCollector as the main entry point and BaseFactCollector managing dependency resolution across platform-specific collectors organized into hardware, network, system, virtual, and other categories.

The key architectural pattern across all subsystems is **platform-specific modularity with fallback mechanisms**: C# and PowerShell utilities mirror Python module_utils for Windows environments, the distro module gracefully degrades to bundled code, and the facts system uses a dependency-aware collector pattern where platform-specific implementations (linux.py, darwin.py, aix.py, etc.) inherit from base classes to gather CPU, memory, networking, virtualization, and distribution information. Critical files include Ansible.Basic.cs (Windows module foundation), Ansible.ModuleUtils.Legacy.psm1 (PowerShell helpers), _distro.py (bundled distribution detector), ansible_collector.py (fact collection orchestrator), and system/distribution.py (distribution file parsing).

agents.name: parsing_and_config
agents.overall_context: Ansible's core parsing and configuration subsystem. This agent owns all YAML parsing logic, vault encryption/decryption handling, parsing utilities, and global configuration management. These components work together to read, validate, and decrypt Ansible playbooks, inventory files, and configuration settings before they reach the executor and playbook orchestration layers.
agents.job_description:
**Parsing and Configuration Subsystem Manager**

I own Ansible's core parsing and configuration infrastructure, responsible for reading, validating, and decrypting all YAML/JSON content before it reaches the executor. The **DataLoader** (lib/ansible/parsing/dataloader.py) is my primary entry point—it loads playbooks, inventory, and variable files with built-in caching and vault decryption support. The **VaultLib** (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py) handles AES256 encryption/decryption using cryptography or pycrypto backends, supporting both legacy and modern vault formats. My **YAML parsing layer** (lib/ansible/parsing/yaml/) uses a custom AnsibleLoader that extends PyYAML with vault-aware constructors and proper error reporting with file positions. The **from_yaml** utility (lib/ansible/parsing/utils/yaml.py) intelligently attempts JSON parsing first, then falls back to YAML, providing unified error handling. On the configuration side, **ConfigManager** (lib/ansible/config/manager.py) reads ansible.cfg files, environment variables, and CLI overrides, while **ConfigData** (lib/ansible/config/data.py) stores both global and plugin-specific settings with type-safe value casting via **ensure_type**. Together, these components form the foundation that all other Ansible subsystems depend on for secure, validated configuration and playbook data.

agents.name: template_and_vars
agents.overall_context: Ansible's template rendering and variable management system. This agent owns the core infrastructure for Jinja2 template processing and variable resolution throughout the playbook execution lifecycle. Templates are used to dynamically generate content in tasks, and vars handles the storage, lookup, and merging of variables from multiple sources (inventory, playbooks, host/group vars, etc.). These two systems are tightly coupled—templates frequently reference variables, and variable resolution often involves template expansion.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own Ansible's template rendering and variable management infrastructure—the core systems that power dynamic content generation and variable resolution throughout playbook execution. The **template** module (lib/ansible/template/) provides the Templar class, which orchestrates Jinja2 template processing with custom variable resolution via AnsibleJ2Vars, unsafe variable tracking, and seamless integration with Ansible's filter, test, and lookup plugins. The **vars** module (lib/ansible/vars/) implements VariableManager, the central hub for variable storage and lookup that enforces strict precedence ordering across multiple sources: role defaults, group/host vars files, inventory, facts, play/task vars, and extra vars. These systems are tightly coupled—templates frequently reference variables through lazy-resolution mappings, and variable expansion often involves template rendering. I manage critical patterns including safe Jinja2 environment configuration, backslash escaping in expressions, unsafe value propagation, fact caching, variable source tracking for debugging, and support for both standard and native Jinja2 modes.

## Job Description

My responsibilities include maintaining module functionality, ensuring idempotency through state parameters and conditional execution patterns, supporting cross-platform compatibility (with platform-specific variants like win_* for Windows), and evolving the module set to meet automation needs. Key entry points include ping.py (connectivity verification), command.py (arbitrary command execution), file.py (file/directory management), setup.py (fact gathering), service.py (service lifecycle management), and apt.py (Debian package management). The **arguments** module (`lib/ansible/cli/arguments/option_helpers.py`) provides reusable components for building consistent argument parsers across all Ansible commands, including custom argparse Actions (AnsibleVersion, PrependListAction, UnrecognizedArgument), a SortingHelpFormatter for organized help output, and builder functions that add standardized option groups (verbosity, async, check, connection, etc.). The **scripts** module (`lib/ansible/cli/scripts/`) contains two critical bootstrap entry points: `ansible_cli_stub.py` dynamically loads and executes CLI command classes based on the invoked script name (e.g., `ansible-playbook` → `PlaybookCLI`), handling argument parsing, error handling, and exit codes; `ansible_connection_cli_stub.py` provides a separate JSON-RPC server for managing persistent connections. agents.job_description:
---

**executor_core** manages the runtime machinery that translates Ansible's parsed playbooks into actual command execution across heterogeneous infrastructure. The domain spans three critical subsystems: **discovery** (platform detection via python_target.py), **process** (task execution via WorkerProcess), and **powershell** (Windows module execution). The core pattern is a multiprocessing architecture where WorkerProcess spawns isolated child processes to execute TaskExecutor for each task, ensuring fault isolation and clean resource cleanup. For Windows targets, PSModuleDepFinder (module_manifest.py) recursively scans PowerShell and C# modules to resolve dependencies declared via #Requires and #AnsibleRequires directives, assembling complete module payloads with utilities and wrapper scripts from the executor/powershell directory (async_wrapper.ps1, become_wrapper.ps1, bootstrap_wrapper.ps1, etc.). Key files include worker.py (process lifecycle and exception handling), module_manifest.py (dependency resolution and module assembly), and python_target.py (platform fact gathering). This layer bridges Ansible's task model with platform-specific execution semantics—Unix process spawning and PowerShell remoting—enabling unified task execution across Windows and Unix targets.

agents.name: execution_plugins

This agent owns action plugins (task execution wrappers), strategy plugins (play execution orchestration), and shell plugins (command execution environments). These work together to define the execution model and task lifecycle.
agents.job_description:
## Execution Plugins Domain Summary

The execution plugins layer controls how Ansible tasks are executed and orchestrated across the infrastructure. This domain consists of three complementary plugin types that work together to define the complete execution model:

**Action Plugins** (`lib/ansible/plugins/action/`) are task execution wrappers that implement the `ActionBase` abstract class. The base class (1,192 lines) provides a comprehensive execution framework with methods for module execution, file operations, command execution, and connection management. Twenty-seven concrete action plugins implement specific Ansible tasks (command, shell, copy, template, debug, assert, etc.), with `normal.py` serving as the default action that delegates to module execution. Action plugins validate task arguments, manage check mode and async support, handle temporary directories, discover interpreters, and orchestrate the full task lifecycle from preparation through result collection.

**Strategy Plugins** (`lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/`) orchestrate play execution and task scheduling across hosts. The `StrategyBase` class (1,329 lines) manages worker processes, task queuing, result aggregation, and handler execution. The `linear.py` strategy (default) executes tasks in lockstep per host batch using the serial parameter, while `free.py` allows independent host execution, and `host_pinned.py` pins tasks to specific hosts. Strategies control task distribution, host state tracking, play progression, and result processing through a sophisticated queuing and worker management system that coordinates execution across multiple hosts and tasks.

**Shell Plugins** (`lib/ansible/plugins/shell/`) define command execution environments and abstract shell-specific syntax differences. The `ShellBase` class (228 lines) provides a unified interface for shell operations including command building, path manipulation, file operations, and temporary directory management. Concrete implementations support POSIX shells (`sh.py`, default), PowerShell, and Windows cmd.exe, each defining shell-specific operators and syntax. Shell plugins generate platform-appropriate commands, manage environment variables, and handle the low-level details of remote command execution, enabling Ansible to work seamlessly across diverse target systems.

agents.overall_context: Ansible connectivity and protocol plugins that manage how Ansible communicates with remote systems. This agent owns connection plugins (SSH, local, etc.), become plugins (privilege escalation), and protocol-specific plugins (CLI config, HTTP API, NETCONF, terminal). These collectively define the transport layer and authentication mechanisms.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's connectivity and protocol plugins that define how Ansible communicates with remote systems. My domain spans six core plugin categories: **Connection plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/connection/) implement transport mechanisms including SSH, Paramiko SSH, local execution, WinRM, and PowerShell Remoting via the ConnectionBase class; **Become plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/become/) handle privilege escalation through sudo, su, and runas via BecomeBase with password prompt detection and success verification; **CLI configuration plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/cliconf/) provide device-specific CLI abstractions for network devices; **HTTP API plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/httpapi/) abstract REST/HTTP-based device communication with authentication and error handling; **NETCONF plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/netconf/) implement NETCONF protocol support for network management; and **Terminal plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/terminal/) manage device-specific terminal behavior, ANSI stripping, and CLI lifecycle hooks.

The key architectural patterns across these plugins are: lazy initialization via decorators (ensure_connect, ensure_ncclient), base class inheritance from AnsiblePlugin, option management with fallback mechanisms, and tight integration between connection and become layers for seamless privilege escalation. Critical files include ConnectionBase (__init__.py, 384 lines), BecomeBase (__init__.py, 108 lines), CliconfBase (__init__.py, 478 lines), HttpApiBase (__init__.py, 87 lines), NetconfBase (__init__.py, 373 lines), and TerminalBase (__init__.py, 134 lines), along with concrete implementations like ssh.py (1255 lines), sudo.py, and device-specific plugins that extend these base classes.

These enable dynamic playbook behavior and data manipulation.
agents.job_description:
I manage Ansible's data processing and templating plugin ecosystem across five specialized plugin categories. **Lookup plugins** (25 plugins) enable dynamic data retrieval during playbook execution from diverse sources—URLs, files, environment variables, CSV/INI files, and custom data structures—through the LookupBase class and its abstract `run()` method. **Inventory plugins** (10 plugins) discover and parse hosts and groups from multiple formats (YAML, INI, scripts, TOML) and sources, providing hostname range expansion, safe group naming, and caching capabilities. **Vars plugins** (2 plugins) load variables for hosts and groups via the BaseVarsPlugin class. **Filter plugins** (4 modules totaling 658+ lines) provide Jinja2 template filters for data transformation including cryptographic hashing, JSON/YAML serialization, regex operations, URL manipulation, and string processing. **Test plugins** (4 modules) implement Jinja2 conditional tests for playbook logic, evaluating task results (failed, success, changed, skipped) and file/math conditions.

The architecture follows consistent patterns: all plugins inherit from AnsiblePlugin, integrate deeply with Jinja2 templating, leverage the loader and templar utilities for file discovery and variable substitution, and use standardized error handling via AnsibleError. Key files include `lib/ansible/plugins/lookup/__init__.py` (LookupBase), `lib/ansible/plugins/inventory/__init__.py` (InventoryBase with 445 lines of helper utilities), `lib/ansible/plugins/filter/core.py` (658-line filter library), and `lib/ansible/plugins/test/core.py` (240-line test library). These plugins collectively enable dynamic, data-driven playbook behavior and sophisticated variable/data manipulation.

## Job Description

I manage Ansible's plugin infrastructure for cross-cutting concerns: callback plugins (event reporting and output formatting), cache plugins (fact caching backends), and doc_fragments (shared documentation for plugin parameters). The callback subsystem provides a base class (CallbackBase in `lib/ansible/plugins/callback/__init__.py`) that plugins inherit to hook into execution events (v2_runner_on_ok, v2_runner_on_failed, etc.) and format output; implementations include default.py, junit.py, minimal.py, oneline.py, and tree.py. The cache subsystem defines abstract base classes (BaseCacheModule and BaseFileCacheModule in `lib/ansible/plugins/cache/__init__.py`) with standard operations (get, set, keys, contains, delete, flush, copy) and concrete backends like memory.py and jsonfile.py for fact persistence.

Doc_fragments in `lib/ansible/plugins/doc_fragments/` provide reusable YAML documentation blocks (ModuleDocFragment classes) that are included via extends_documentation_fragment directives; key fragments include default_callback.py (display options for callbacks) and inventory_cache.py (cache configuration options). The infrastructure emphasizes plugin option management through set_options/get_option patterns, configuration via environment variables and ini files, and consistent error handling. These three domains work together to enable extensible, configurable event handling and data persistence across Ansible's execution lifecycle.

agents.name: inventory_management

It bridges configuration input with the executor and plugin systems, ensuring hosts are properly resolved and grouped before playbook execution.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

The Inventory Management system is the foundational layer that parses, loads, and maintains all host and group definitions from diverse sources (static files, dynamic scripts, cloud providers, etc.). Centered around the **InventoryManager** class (manager.py), it orchestrates multi-source parsing via a plugin-based architecture, populating an **InventoryData** structure containing **Host** and **Group** objects with hierarchical relationships. The system handles sophisticated host pattern matching with subscripts, intersections, and exclusions (e.g., `webservers[0:5]`, `&prod`, `!deprecated`), maintains dual-level caching for performance, and merges variables from multiple sources (inventory files, group_vars, host_vars directories) into a unified variable namespace. Key responsibilities include resolving host patterns to concrete host lists, managing group hierarchies with parent-child relationships, creating implicit localhost for local execution, and providing the core data structures that feed into the execution pipeline.

agents.name: parsing_core
agents.overall_context: Ansible's parsing subsystem is responsible for reading, validating, and processing configuration files, playbooks, and inventory data. This agent owns the core parsing infrastructure including YAML parsing (the primary format for Ansible), vault decryption for encrypted content, and utility functions that support parsing operations. The parsing layer is foundational—it sits between raw file I/O and the execution engine, transforming user-provided configuration into structured data that the rest of Ansible consumes. This agent ensures that all input formats are correctly interpreted and that sensitive data (vault-encrypted content) is properly handled throughout the parsing pipeline.
agents.job_description: The parsing_core subsystem is the foundational layer responsible for transforming raw configuration files, playbooks, and inventory data into structured Python objects that Ansible's execution engine consumes. It manages three critical responsibilities: YAML/JSON parsing with a custom AnsibleLoader that extends PyYAML to support Ansible-specific types and vault-encrypted content, vault decryption using AES256 encryption with cryptography library support (falling back to pycrypto), and argument parsing for the multiple syntaxes Ansible supports for module invocation. The DataLoader class serves as the primary facade, providing file loading with intelligent caching, path resolution, and seamless vault integration. The architecture follows a layered pattern where YAML parsing happens through a custom constructor that intercepts vault-encrypted values during object construction, while argument parsing handles both structured (YAML dict) and unstructured (key=value) module parameters. Key files include dataloader.py (main entry point), yaml/loader.py and yaml/constructor.py (custom YAML infrastructure), vault/__init__.py (encryption/decryption engine), and mod_args.py/splitter.py (argument parsing). The subsystem prioritizes security by detecting and decrypting vault content transparently, performance through file caching, and compatibility by supporting both JSON and YAML formats with JSON attempted first for extra vars.

agents.name: playbook_execution
agents.overall_context: Ansible playbook execution layer. This agent owns the playbook parsing, role loading, task orchestration, and play execution logic. It bridges between the parsing layer (which produces AST) and the executor core (which runs tasks). Playbooks are the primary user-facing abstraction in Ansible—they define what gets executed and in what order. Roles are reusable collections of tasks, handlers, variables, and templates that playbooks reference. This agent handles the structural interpretation and sequencing of playbook/role definitions.
agents.job_description:
---

**PLAYBOOK EXECUTION LAYER - Structural Interpretation & Sequencing**

I manage the parsing, loading, and structural organization of Ansible playbooks and roles—the primary user-facing abstractions that define what gets executed and in what order. The layer bridges between the YAML parsing layer (which produces raw data structures) and the executor core (which runs tasks). Key components include: **Playbook** (top-level container that loads YAML files and parses plays/includes), **Play** (a list of roles and task blocks targeting specific hosts), **Task** (module invocations with arguments, loops, retries, delegation), **Block** (task grouping with rescue/always error handling), and **Role** (reusable collections of tasks, handlers, variables, and templates).

The architecture centers on a declarative **attribute system** using Python metaclasses (base.py, FieldAttribute) that enables inheritance, validation, and post-processing across all playbook objects. A consistent **load pattern** uses static `.load()` methods to parse YAML into typed objects with variable and loader dependencies. The hierarchy flows Playbook → Play → Block → Task, with Roles injected at the Play level, and parent references enable variable/attribute inheritance throughout. Helper functions (helpers.py) handle list parsing and implicit block squashing for efficiency. All executable objects support **Conditional** and **Taggable** mixins for when-clauses and tag filtering. Critical files: base.py (attribute metaclass system), play.py (play definition), task.py (task/module execution), block.py (error handling), role/__init__.py (role management), and helpers.py (list loading utilities).

agents.name: module_utils_core
agents.overall_context: Ansible module utilities provide shared helper functions and compatibility layers for all module implementations. This agent owns the foundational utilities: common helpers (18 files), Python 2/3 compatibility shims (5 files), parsing utilities (2 files), and six library integration (1 file). These are cross-cutting concerns used by modules across all platforms and are tightly coupled to Ansible's module execution model.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the foundational utilities layer for Ansible module execution, providing cross-cutting concerns used by all module implementations across all platforms. My domain spans four key areas: **common utilities** (18 files) including parameter validation, type checking, collections abstractions, text/byte conversions, and platform-specific helpers; **Python 2/3 compatibility shims** (5 files) providing backports of selectors, importlib, and paramiko; **parsing utilities** (2 files) for boolean conversion; and the **vendored six library** (1 file, 963 lines) offering fundamental type abstractions and version checks. The key patterns I enforce are: (1) strict Python 2/3 compatibility through six and custom shims, (2) parameter validation and transformation for module argument specs, (3) safe type conversions with error handling, and (4) immutable data structures for security-sensitive contexts. Critical files include `validation.py` (parameter checking), `parameters.py` (module context handling), `text/converters.py` (encoding/decoding), `collections.py` (ImmutableDict), and `six/__init__.py` (type abstractions). These utilities are tightly coupled to Ansible's module execution model and form the bedrock upon which all module implementations depend.

agents.name: module_utils_facts
agents.overall_context: The facts subsystem (70 files with subfolders) is a substantial, self-contained component responsible for gathering and managing system facts across different platforms and distributions. It handles discovery, caching, and normalization of system information that modules rely on for conditional logic and configuration. This agent owns the entire facts infrastructure including platform-specific fact collectors.
agents.job_description: The module_utils/facts subsystem is a comprehensive, modular infrastructure for gathering and managing system information across multiple platforms and distributions. It implements a pluggable collector pattern where each fact collector (hardware, network, system, virtual, etc.) inherits from BaseFactCollector and implements a collect() method that returns a dictionary of facts. The system supports platform-specific implementations for Linux, Darwin, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly, AIX, HPUX, Hurd, and SunOS, with ~70 total collector classes organized into categories: base (platform/distribution), restrictive (SELinux/AppArmor), general (Python/packages/services), virtual, hardware, network, and external sources (Facter/Ohai). Key features include dependency resolution between collectors, namespace transformation for fact names (e.g., adding 'ansible_' prefix), gather subset filtering allowing users to request 'all', 'min', specific subsets, or exclusions, and timeout management. The main entry point is get_ansible_collector() in ansible_collector.py, which orchestrates the AnsibleFactCollector to run selected collectors in dependency order and return normalized facts under the 'ansible_facts' key.

## Job Description

I manage platform-specific module utilities that enable Ansible to work across heterogeneous infrastructure. My domain spans three critical areas: **C# helpers** (6 files) for Windows module development including the core AnsibleModule class, privilege escalation, and Windows API interop; **PowerShell utilities** (12 files) for PS module execution covering command execution, file operations, privilege management, and legacy compatibility; and **distro detection** (2 files) for reliable Linux OS identification. The key patterns I maintain are: P/Invoke interop abstractions for Windows APIs, dual-runtime support for both .NET Framework and PowerShell Core with conditional compilation symbols, and a bundled distro library with normalization tables for cross-platform OS detection.

The critical entry points are Ansible.Basic.cs (core module initialization and result handling), Ansible.ModuleUtils.Legacy.psm1 (backward-compatible PS helpers), Ansible.ModuleUtils.AddType.psm1 (C# compilation wrapper), and the distro compat wrapper in __init__.py that gracefully falls back to bundled detection when the system package is unavailable. These utilities form the foundation enabling Windows, Linux, and cross-platform module development throughout Ansible.

It handles downloading, installing, and managing community and official Ansible content from the Galaxy repository.
agents.job_description: The Galaxy Management subagent owns Ansible's package management and distribution system for community and official Ansible content. It manages the complete lifecycle of roles and collections—from API communication with Galaxy servers (supporting v1, v2, and v3 endpoints) to downloading, installing, and resolving dependencies. The core architecture centers on three primary content types: the GalaxyAPI client (api.py) handles all server communication with lazy-initialized version negotiation, the CollectionRequirement class (collection.py) manages collection metadata, dependency resolution, and installation workflows, and the GalaxyRole class (role.py) handles traditional role management. Supporting infrastructure includes token-based authentication (token.py, login.py) for secure API access, a Galaxy class (\_\_init\_\_.py) that manages global configuration and role paths, and a comprehensive data directory containing Jinja2 templates for scaffolding new roles and collections across multiple types (standard, network, container, and APB). Key patterns include decorator-based API version negotiation, tarball-based content distribution with SHA256 verification, and multi-threaded dependency resolution for efficient installation.

agents.name: configuration_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible configuration management system. This agent owns the central configuration module that handles loading, parsing, and managing Ansible's configuration settings (ansible.cfg, environment variables, defaults). It serves as the foundational configuration layer that other components depend on for runtime behavior, defaults, and user-customizable settings. This is typically one of the first modules initialized during Ansible startup.
agents.job_description:
---

**Configuration Management Module - Core Ansible Configuration System**

I manage Ansible's foundational configuration layer, responsible for loading, parsing, and resolving all configuration settings from multiple sources (ansible.cfg files, environment variables, and built-in defaults). The ConfigManager class is the primary entry point, initialized early during Ansible startup, and orchestrates a three-tier resolution hierarchy: environment variables → INI/YAML configuration files → hardcoded defaults. I handle sophisticated type coercion (boolean, integer, float, list, path, pathlist, pathspec, tmppath, string), plugin-scoped configuration overrides, and setting origin tracking to record where each value came from.

The module's architecture centers on three key components: **manager.py** (ConfigManager class with parsing and value resolution logic), **data.py** (ConfigData container for storing global and plugin-specific settings), and **base.yml** (comprehensive YAML definitions of all 200+ Ansible configuration options with metadata). I also manage plugin routing for backwards compatibility and module default groupings. Configuration file discovery follows a strict precedence: ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable → current working directory → user home directory → system-wide /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg, with security checks to prevent loading from world-writable directories.

agents.name: template_rendering
agents.overall_context: Ansible's template rendering engine. This agent owns the Jinja2-based templating system that processes variable substitution, filters, and dynamic content generation across playbooks, roles, and task execution. It handles template compilation, caching, and the runtime environment for safe template evaluation.
agents.job_description:
---

**TEMPLATE RENDERING ENGINE - Jinja2-Based Templating System**

I manage Ansible's Jinja2-based template rendering engine, which processes variable substitution, filters, and dynamic content generation across playbooks, roles, and task execution. The core architecture centers on the **Templar** class (lib/ansible/template/__init__.py, 945 lines) as the primary entry point, which orchestrates template compilation, caching, and safe runtime evaluation. Key supporting components include **AnsibleJ2Vars** for lazy variable resolution with unsafe tracking, **AnsibleContext** for propagating unsafe values through variable lookups, **AnsibleEnvironment** for custom Jinja2 configuration, and **JinjaPluginIntercept** for dynamic collection-based filter/test loading.

The system implements several critical patterns: lazy evaluation of variables to prevent premature templating, SHA1-based result caching to optimize repeated renders, unsafe value propagation through context resolution, backslash escaping to handle multiple parsing layers (YAML→Python→Jinja2), and type preservation for bare variable references. Supporting utilities include **safe_eval** (safe_eval.py) for whitelisted Python expression evaluation, **native_helpers** (native_helpers.py) for native Python type conversion when enabled, and **AnsibleJ2Template** (template.py) to prevent dict conversion of variable storage during includes. This architecture ensures safe, efficient, and type-preserving template rendering across Ansible's execution model.

agents.name: utility_functions
agents.overall_context: Ansible's general-purpose utility library providing cross-cutting helper functions, data structures, and common operations used throughout the codebase. This agent owns shared utility code that supports parsing, execution, plugin infrastructure, and other core systems. It serves as a foundational layer that multiple other agents depend on.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

The utility_functions agent manages Ansible's foundational utility library (`lib/ansible/utils`), providing cross-cutting helper functions, data structures, and common operations used throughout the codebase. This module serves as a critical infrastructure layer supporting parsing, execution, plugin infrastructure, and core system operations. Key responsibilities include maintaining the Singleton metaclass pattern for stateful utilities (Display, AnsibleCollectionLoader, context objects), managing data transformation utilities (path canonicalization, list deduplication, type conversions), providing security and cryptography functions (password encryption, hashing), and ensuring Python 2/3 compatibility. The library emphasizes immutable data structures for configuration safety, centralized output handling through the Display class with terminal color support, and consistent error handling via AnsibleError.

agents.name: variable_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible's variable management system. This module handles the core logic for variable storage, resolution, and scoping across playbook execution. It manages variable precedence, templating context, and the variable namespace that playbooks and tasks operate within. Works closely with the parsing system (YAML/vault) and playbook execution engine to provide variables at runtime.
agents.job_description: The Ansible variable management system is the core engine for variable storage, resolution, and scoping throughout playbook execution. The **VariableManager** class (manager.py) orchestrates a multi-layered caching system that maintains variables across different scopes: persistent fact caches, host/group variable files, play-level variables, task-level variables, and extra variables. It implements a strict precedence hierarchy where role defaults take highest priority, followed by group/host variables, facts, play variables, task variables, and finally extra variables. The system integrates tightly with the **HostVars** mapping (hostvars.py) for lazy-loaded host variable access, the **FactCache** (fact_cache.py) for persistent fact storage via pluggable backends, and variable plugins (plugins.py) for extensible variable source loading at inventory and task execution stages. Supporting modules handle variable cleaning (clean.py) to sanitize internal metadata, reserved name validation (reserved.py) to prevent namespace conflicts, and source tracking for debugging. The architecture emphasizes performance through caching and lazy evaluation while maintaining strict variable isolation and precedence semantics required for complex multi-host playbook execution.

agents.name: cli_tests
agents.overall_context: Unit tests for Ansible CLI interface and argument parsing. This agent owns all CLI-related test coverage, complementing the cli_interface agent that covers the actual CLI implementation. Tests validate command-line argument handling, help text, and CLI entry points.
agents.job_description:

agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the code-smell sanity checks for the Ansible codebase, a collection of 12 specialized Python validators that detect structural and quality issues early in the development pipeline. Each check consists of a paired Python script and JSON configuration file that validates specific aspects of code quality: BOTMETA.yml metadata structure, changelog file formats, file extension compliance, package distribution integrity, deprecated configuration usage, and module attribute patterns. The checks follow a consistent pattern—reading file paths from command-line arguments or stdin and outputting errors in standardized "path:line:column:message" format for integration with the sanity test framework.

The key patterns I enforce include metadata validation using voluptuous schemas (botmeta.py), changelog extension enforcement (changelog.py), prevention of unwanted file types in the source tree (no-unwanted-files.py), verification of package data integrity for distribution (package-data.py), and detection of improper FieldAttribute usage in module definitions (required-and-default-attributes.py). Two checks (deprecated-config.py and update-bundled.py) are disabled by default in skip.txt, reserved for release managers to enable after branching. These checks collectively ensure code consistency, prevent common mistakes, and maintain the structural integrity of the Ansible project across its entire codebase.

agents.name: cli_interface
agents.overall_context: Ansible command-line interface layer. Owns argument parsing, CLI script entry points, and user-facing command handling. This agent is responsible for translating user input into executable operations and managing the CLI experience.
agents.job_description: The CLI Interface Layer manages Ansible's command-line experience through a modular, template-method architecture. The base CLI class in `lib/ansible/cli/__init__.py` provides the parsing orchestration framework that all Ansible tools (playbook, adhoc, vault, galaxy, etc.) inherit from. Each CLI subclass defines its specific options via composable helper functions in `lib/ansible/cli/arguments/option_helpers.py`, which centralizes argument definitions to prevent duplication. The entry point dispatcher in `lib/ansible/cli/scripts/ansible_cli_stub.py` dynamically routes commands to the appropriate CLI class based on the executable name, handling Python version validation and error management with specific exit codes. The layer translates raw command-line arguments into a structured context (context.CLIARGS) that downstream components access globally, while supporting advanced features like vault secret management, password prompts, inventory defaults, and shell tab-completion via argcomplete.

agents.name: task_execution
agents.overall_context: Ansible task execution engine. Owns the runtime machinery for discovering targets, executing tasks across platforms (including PowerShell), and managing process lifecycle. This agent handles the core execution logic that transforms playbook directives into actual system operations.
agents.job_description: The Ansible Task Execution Engine manages the runtime machinery that transforms playbook directives into actual system operations across distributed hosts. It implements a hierarchical multiprocessing architecture where PlaybookExecutor orchestrates TaskQueueManager, which spawns WorkerProcess instances that each run TaskExecutor to dispatch individual tasks to hosts via pluggable action plugins. The engine handles cross-platform execution through interpreter discovery (Python bootstrap + platform detection), PowerShell module dependency scanning with C# utility support, and connection/shell/become plugin abstraction. Key patterns include queue-based inter-process communication, result aggregation with state tracking (changed/failed/skipped/unreachable), task looping and squashing optimizations, and comprehensive lifecycle management from playbook parsing through execution completion.

agents.name: playbook_orchestration
agents.overall_context: Ansible playbook and role orchestration layer. Owns playbook parsing, role management, and the structural organization of automation workflows. This agent defines how tasks are grouped, sequenced, and reused through roles.
agents.job_description: The Playbook Orchestration Layer manages the structural organization and execution sequencing of Ansible automation workflows. It owns the hierarchical composition of playbooks into plays, blocks, and tasks, with a sophisticated attribute-driven design pattern using FieldAttribute metaclasses for declarative field definitions. The layer handles role management through RoleDefinition and RoleInclude classes that resolve role paths, split parameters, and support collection references. Key patterns include lazy loading of roles and includes, implicit block wrapping of bare tasks, and attribute inheritance flowing from plays down through blocks to individual tasks. The core entry points—Playbook, Play, Block, and Task—work together with helper functions like load_list_of_blocks to parse YAML structures and construct executable object graphs, while mixins like Conditional, Taggable, and CollectionSearch provide cross-cutting concerns for filtering, conditional execution, and collection resolution across the entire orchestration hierarchy.

agents.name: action_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible action plugins are the core execution layer that translates task directives into module invocations and handles task-level logic. This agent owns all built-in action plugins that implement task behaviors like copy, template, command execution, and async handling. Action plugins bridge the playbook execution engine and module execution, making this a critical and self-contained domain.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

The action plugins domain manages the core execution layer that translates Ansible task directives into module invocations and handles task-level logic. This domain owns 27 built-in action plugins that implement critical task behaviors including file operations (copy, template, fetch, assemble, unarchive), command execution (command, shell, raw, script), system management (service, package, reboot), control flow (debug, fail, assert, pause), inventory manipulation (add_host, group_by, set_fact), and async handling. All plugins inherit from ActionBase, a 1192-line abstract base class defined in `__init__.py` that provides connection management, module configuration and execution, remote file operations, async/check-mode support, and temporary path management.

The domain follows consistent patterns: each plugin implements a `run(tmp, task_vars)` method that calls `super().run()` for validation, then performs task-specific logic before delegating to `_execute_module()` for actual module execution. Key architectural features include argument validation via `_VALID_ARGS`, async wrapping for connections without native async support, check mode enforcement, and interpreter discovery. Complex plugins like copy.py (595 lines) handle directory walking and checksumming, while simpler ones like normal.py (58 lines) provide minimal wrapping. This domain is self-contained and critical to Ansible's execution model, bridging the playbook engine and module execution.

agents.name: lookup_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible lookup plugins provide dynamic data retrieval and templating capabilities during playbook execution. This agent owns all built-in lookup plugins (file, env, template, etc.) that enable users to fetch configuration, secrets, and computed values at runtime. Lookups are a self-contained plugin category with clear boundaries and no overlap with other plugin types.
agents.job_description:
---

**Lookup Plugins Domain Specialist**

I manage all 25 built-in Ansible lookup plugins located in `lib/ansible/plugins/lookup/`, which provide dynamic data retrieval and templating capabilities during playbook execution. These plugins enable users to fetch configuration files, environment variables, secrets, computed values, and remote data at runtime through a consistent interface. The domain is self-contained with clear boundaries—lookups are invoked via the `lookup()` function in Jinja2 templates and do not overlap with other plugin types like modules, filters, or inventory plugins.

All lookup plugins inherit from the `LookupBase` class defined in `__init__.py` (lines 33-126) and implement a `run(terms, variables, **kwargs)` method that processes input terms and returns results. Key patterns include: standardized DOCUMENTATION/EXAMPLES/RETURN metadata blocks, utility methods for flattening and combining data structures, file search path resolution, and templating support. Core plugins include `file` (read controller files), `env` (environment variables), `template` (Jinja2 processing), `vars` (variable lookup), and `url` (HTTP requests), alongside specialized plugins for CSV parsing, INI files, password generation, shell pipes, sequences, and inventory operations. Each plugin is self-contained and independently testable, with the framework handling plugin discovery and invocation.

agents.name: inventory_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible inventory plugins dynamically discover and populate host and group information from various sources (cloud providers, databases, files, APIs). This agent owns all built-in inventory plugins that enable flexible infrastructure representation. Inventory plugins are foundational to playbook execution, providing the host graph that tasks operate against.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage all built-in inventory plugins for Ansible, which are the foundational mechanisms for dynamically discovering and populating host and group information from diverse sources. The inventory plugins directory contains 10 core plugins that parse inventory data from various formats (YAML, INI, JSON, comma-separated lists, scripts, TOML) and sources (files, APIs, cloud providers, databases). All plugins inherit from `BaseInventoryPlugin` (defined in `__init__.py`), implementing the standard `parse()` and `verify_file()` interface, and support optional caching and Jinja2 templating via the `Templar` class. The `auto.py` plugin acts as a meta-dispatcher, automatically detecting and delegating to the appropriate plugin based on configuration, enabling seamless plugin chaining. Key patterns include hostname range expansion (e.g., `web[1:10]`), group name sanitization, variable composition, and dynamic group construction. The plugins are essential to playbook execution, as they construct the host graph that all tasks operate against, supporting flexible infrastructure representation across on-premises, cloud, and hybrid environments.

agents.name: connection_and_transport
agents.overall_context: Ansible connection and transport plugins handle communication with remote systems across diverse protocols and device types. This agent owns connection plugins (SSH, local, paramiko), shell plugins (bash, powershell, cmd), and protocol-specific plugins (netconf, cliconf, httpapi, terminal). Together they form the transport abstraction layer that enables Ansible to work with any infrastructure type.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own Ansible's transport abstraction layer—the connection and protocol plugins that enable communication with any infrastructure type. My domain spans six plugin categories: **connection plugins** (SSH, local, paramiko, WinRM, PSRP) that establish and manage remote sessions; **shell plugins** (sh, PowerShell, cmd) that abstract shell-specific command syntax and file operations; and **protocol-specific plugins** (terminal, cliconf, netconf, httpapi) that provide structured interfaces for network devices and APIs. The core architecture centers on `ConnectionBase` (lib/ansible/plugins/connection/__init__.py, line 39) which defines the transport contract with methods like `_connect()`, `exec_command()`, `put_file()`, and `fetch_file()`, while `ShellBase` (lib/ansible/plugins/shell/__init__.py, line 35) abstracts shell operations like command building, temp directory creation, and file permissions. Key patterns include: decorator-based auto-connection (`ensure_connect`), lazy shell plugin loading, support for pipelining and native async, and privilege escalation hooks for become plugins.

For network automation, I provide specialized layers: `TerminalBase` for interactive CLI device sessions with prompt handling and ANSI stripping; `CliconfBase` for structured CLI command execution with config get/edit operations; `NetconfBase` for XML-RPC device configuration via ncclient; and `HttpApiBase` for REST API device communication with session and error handling. Together, these plugins form a unified transport abstraction that lets Ansible work seamlessly across Unix/Linux systems, Windows hosts, and network devices via CLI, NETCONF, or HTTP APIs.

agents.name: execution_control
agents.overall_context: Ansible execution control plugins manage how tasks are scheduled and executed across hosts, and how privilege escalation is handled. This agent owns strategy plugins (linear, free, debug) that determine task execution order and parallelism, and become plugins (sudo, su, doas) that handle privilege elevation. Together they control the execution model and security posture of playbook runs.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's execution control layer, which determines how tasks are scheduled, executed, and privileged across hosts. The **strategy plugins** (linear, free, debug, host_pinned) control task execution order and parallelism by inheriting from StrategyBase (lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/__init__.py, 1329 lines), which orchestrates task queuing, worker process management, result collection via background threads, and interactive debugging. The **become plugins** (sudo, su, runas) handle privilege escalation by inheriting from BecomeBase (lib/ansible/plugins/become/__init__.py, 108 lines), which builds privilege-escalated commands, detects password prompts, verifies execution success via markers, and handles i18n error messages. Together, these plugins define Ansible's execution model—whether tasks run in lockstep (linear), in parallel (free), or pinned to workers (host_pinned)—and its security posture through configurable privilege elevation mechanisms.

agents.name: data_processing
agents.overall_context: Ansible data processing plugins provide templating, validation, and variable management capabilities. This agent owns filter plugins (Jinja2 filters for data transformation), test plugins (conditional tests for assertions), and vars plugins (dynamic variable loading). Together they enable rich data manipulation and validation within playbooks.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's data processing plugins across three core domains: **filter plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/filter/), **test plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/test/), and **vars plugins** (lib/ansible/plugins/vars/). Filter plugins provide Jinja2 filters for data transformation—including type conversions (to_yaml, to_json, to_bool), string operations (regex_replace, quote), hashing (md5, sha1, password_hash), and collection operations (flatten, combine, extract, dict2items)—with specialized modules for math and URL handling. Test plugins enable conditional assertions on task results and data validation, covering task state tests (failed, changed, skipped), async status checks, regex matching, version comparison, and truthiness evaluation.
