agents.overall_context: Ansible's internal serialization layer for JSON and YAML data handling. These modules provide low-level parsing, encoding, and data transformation utilities that support the broader parsing_and_serialization agent but operate at the internal implementation level. This agent handles format-specific serialization concerns that are used throughout Ansible's execution pipeline.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

The internal_serialization agent manages Ansible's low-level JSON and YAML serialization infrastructure, providing format-specific parsing, encoding, and data transformation utilities that underpin the broader parsing_and_serialization pipeline. The JSON module (`lib/ansible/_internal/_json`) centers on the `AnsibleVariableVisitor` class—a recursive visitor pattern implementation that enforces Ansible's variable type system, handles encrypted strings with configurable behaviors (decrypt/redact/preserve/fail), applies template trust tagging, and performs origin tracking across complex data structures. It also provides legacy JSON encoding support for backward compatibility with vault value conversion and trust stripping. The YAML module (`lib/ansible/_internal/_yaml`) implements custom YAML parsing and serialization through `AnsibleInstrumentedLoader` and `AnsibleDumper`, which integrate origin tagging and template trust metadata into the parse/dump cycle, while `AnsibleInstrumentedConstructor` handles YAML node construction with duplicate key detection. Critical to both modules is sophisticated error handling: the YAML error handler (`AnsibleYAMLParserError`) performs regex-based analysis to detect and provide helpful guidance for common mistakes like unquoted templates, unquoted colons, mismatched quotes, and tab characters, enriching error context with precise source locations.

agents.name: internal_utilities
agents.overall_context: Ansible's core internal utility modules that provide foundational services used across the entire codebase. This includes error handling, data tagging, encryption, SSH protocol support, templating engines, and plugin infrastructure. These utilities are low-level building blocks that support higher-level agents like playbook_execution, connectivity_protocols, and execution_control.
agents.job_description: Internal Utilities manages Ansible's foundational infrastructure layer, providing six critical subsystems that enable higher-level components to function reliably. The domain encompasses data tagging for forensic provenance tracking (Origin, TrustedAsTemplate), cryptographic abstractions with platform-specific library handling, comprehensive error handling with structured exception factories and configurable error actions, plugin infrastructure for transparent data serialization, SSH protocol support with agent management, and an advanced Jinja2 templating engine with lazy evaluation and custom markers. These utilities follow consistent patterns: dataclass-based configuration, context managers for flow control, lazy evaluation to defer expensive operations, marker-based error handling to capture exceptions without raising, and platform-specific abstractions to handle environmental variations. Key files include _datatag/_tags.py (Origin metadata), _encryption/_crypt.py (CryptFacade), _errors/_error_factory.py and _handler.py (EventFactory and ErrorHandler), _plugins/_cache.py (PluginInterposer), _ssh/_ssh_agent.py (SSH agent management), and _templating/_engine.py and _jinja_bits.py (Jinja2 customization). These low-level building blocks are consumed by higher-level agents managing playbook execution, connectivity protocols, and execution control.

agents.name: collection_management
agents.overall_context: Internal collection management and discovery infrastructure. This module supports the galaxy_management agent by providing low-level collection handling, metadata processing, and collection-related utilities that enable Ansible to work with collections at runtime.
agents.job_description: The collection_management subagent manages the internal "Protomatter" collection embedded within ansible-core—an unsupported, unstable collection designed exclusively for ansible-core's integration tests and debugging purposes. This module provides specialized plugins that expose internal templating, data tagging, and configuration introspection capabilities that are not available through standard Ansible mechanisms. The collection contains four plugin categories: action plugins (debug.py) for raw expression evaluation without template processing; filter plugins (apply_trust, dump_object, finalize, origin, python_literal_eval, tag_names, true_type, unmask) for data transformation and trust marking; lookup plugins (config) for specialized configuration access; and test plugins (tagged, tagged_with) for inspecting data tag metadata. All plugins directly integrate with ansible-core's internal templating engine, data tagging system, and configuration infrastructure, making them critical for testing and troubleshooting core functionality while remaining explicitly unsupported for external use.

agents.name: variable_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible's variable management system handles the storage, resolution, and lifecycle of variables across playbook execution. This agent owns the core variable infrastructure that supports dynamic inventory data, host/group variables, and runtime variable substitution. It integrates with the inventory system (which provides host/group structure), the playbook executor (which consumes resolved variables), and the parsing layer (which deserializes variable data from YAML/JSON sources). The vars module is foundational to Ansible's templating and variable precedence system.
agents.job_description: The Variable Management System (lib/ansible/vars) is the foundational infrastructure for Ansible's variable storage, resolution, and lifecycle management. It owns the VariableManager class, which orchestrates variable precedence across multiple sources—role defaults, group/host variables, facts, play/task variables, and extra vars—implementing a strict hierarchical merge strategy. The system integrates deeply with the inventory system (providing host/group structure), the playbook executor (consuming resolved variables), and the templating engine (expanding variable references). Key components include HostVars for lazy host-scoped variable access, plugin orchestration for dynamic variable loading at inventory and task stages, fact sanitization and caching mechanisms, and reserved name validation to prevent shadowing of Jinja2 globals and playbook attributes. The module implements sophisticated caching strategies (fact_cache, vars_cache, plugin LRU) and manages variable lifecycle through multiple execution stages while maintaining backward compatibility through deprecation tracking.

agents.name: test_infrastructure
agents.overall_context: Ansible's testing framework and infrastructure. This agent owns the test harness that enables ansible_test to run unit tests, integration tests, sanity checks, and other validation across the codebase. It provides utilities for test execution, data fixtures, configuration management, and internal testing helpers. This is the backbone of Ansible's quality assurance pipeline.
agents.job_description:
Test Infrastructure Domain Specialist

I manage Ansible's comprehensive testing framework and quality assurance pipeline. My domain encompasses the `ansible_test` command-line tool and its supporting infrastructure across four key areas: the core execution engine (`_internal`), utility tools (`_util`), test data and fixtures (`_data`), and configuration templates (`config`). The system orchestrates unit tests, integration tests, sanity checks, and coverage analysis through a command-driven architecture with sophisticated test target classification, host provisioning, and result aggregation. Key patterns include a configuration hierarchy using dataclasses, change-based test filtering with confidence scoring, distributed test delegation across hosts, and extensive use of provisioning profiles for Docker, SSH, and controller environments. Critical entry points are the main() function in `__init__.py`, CLI argument parsing in `cli/__init__.py`, command implementations in `commands/`, and the executor module that handles test execution and change detection. The infrastructure provides comprehensive utilities for test execution including pytest plugins, sanity check implementations, bootstrap scripts, and playbooks for host setup across POSIX and Windows platforms.

agents.name: cli_interface
agents.overall_context: Ansible command-line interface layer. This agent owns the CLI argument parsing and script execution infrastructure that forms the entry point for Ansible commands. It handles command-line argument definitions, validation, and the scripts that bootstrap CLI operations.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the Ansible command-line interface argument parsing and script execution infrastructure. My domain spans two key areas: **lib/ansible/cli/arguments** provides the argument parsing layer through a custom ArgumentParser class (option_helpers.py) that extends argparse with deprecation tracking, argument tagging for data provenance, help text enhancement, and pre-built option groups (verbosity, async, connection, check, basedir). I handle version display with git repository information, path normalization via unfrack_path callbacks, and custom actions for specialized argument handling like PrependListAction and AnsibleVersion. **lib/ansible/cli/scripts** manages the execution infrastructure, specifically persistent connection management through ansible_connection_cli_stub.py, which implements a ConnectionProcess class that establishes Unix socket-based communication with remote devices, handles JSON-RPC request/response cycles, manages signal-based timeouts, and maintains connection lifecycle across playbook execution.

The key patterns I manage are: (1) argument validation and deprecation warnings with version tracking, (2) path normalization and expansion for Ansible's file system operations, (3) persistent connection lifecycle management with socket-based IPC, (4) signal-based timeout handling for connection operations, and (5) JSON-RPC protocol implementation for remote device communication. Critical files include option_helpers.py (556 lines) for argument infrastructure and ansible_connection_cli_stub.py (343 lines) for connection process management.

agents.name: task_execution_engine
agents.overall_context: Ansible's core task execution layer. This agent owns the runtime machinery that discovers available modules, executes tasks across different platforms (with specialized PowerShell support for Windows), and manages subprocess lifecycle. It bridges the gap between parsed playbooks/roles and actual system-level command execution, handling platform-specific execution strategies and process management.
agents.job_description: The task execution engine manages three critical runtime layers that bridge parsed playbooks to actual system-level command execution. The **process layer** (worker.py) provides multiprocessing infrastructure through WorkerProcess, a subprocess wrapper that instantiates TaskExecutor, manages signal handling, detaches stdio, and serializes task results back to the parent strategy layer—ensuring complete process isolation to prevent exceptions from corrupting the parent. The **PowerShell layer** (module_manifest.py and 14 wrapper scripts) handles Windows-specific execution with PSModuleDepFinder for discovering and bundling PowerShell module dependencies, C# utilities, and base64-encoded scripts into execution manifests, while specialized wrappers (exec_wrapper.ps1, async_wrapper.ps1, become_wrapper.ps1) manage module invocation, asynchronous operations, privilege escalation, and file transfer protocols (WinRM, PSRP). The **discovery layer** (currently minimal) is designated for module discovery mechanisms that locate available modules across the system. Key patterns include subprocess lifecycle management with signal propagation, platform-specific execution strategies (Unix vs. Windows), dependency manifest generation, and queue-based inter-process communication for results and display output.

agents.name: inventory_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible's inventory system is responsible for parsing, loading, and managing host and group definitions from various sources (static files, dynamic scripts, cloud providers, etc.). This agent owns the core inventory parsing, caching, and querying logic that feeds into task execution. It bridges user-provided inventory data with the task execution engine, ensuring hosts and groups are properly resolved before playbook execution.
agents.job_description:
---

**Inventory Management System**

The inventory management subsystem is the core data layer that parses, loads, and maintains all host and group definitions for Ansible playbook execution. It owns the InventoryManager class (manager.py) which orchestrates parsing from multiple sources via pluggable inventory plugins, manages caching of resolved host patterns, and provides the query interface for task execution. The system is built on three foundational object types—InventoryData (data.py) which holds the host/group graph, Host (host.py) representing individual targets with variables and group membership, and Group (group.py) representing hierarchical host collections with parent-child relationships and variable inheritance. Key patterns include sophisticated host pattern matching with subscripts and set operations (wildcards, ranges, intersections, exclusions), multi-level variable inheritance from groups to hosts, implicit localhost creation with local connection defaults, and post-parsing reconciliation to ensure inventory consistency. The system caches resolved patterns for performance and integrates with the vars plugin system to load group_vars and host_vars from external sources.

agents.name: action_plugins
agents.overall_context: Ansible action plugins are the core execution layer that translates task directives into concrete operations on target systems. This agent owns all built-in action plugins (29 files) that handle task execution, module invocation, and result processing. Action plugins bridge the gap between the task definition and the actual module execution, managing things like async operations, delegation, and result transformation.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own the action plugins subsystem—the 29 built-in action plugins that form Ansible's core execution layer. Action plugins translate task directives into concrete operations on target systems by bridging task definitions and module execution. The foundation is **ActionBase** (`__init__.py`, 1437 lines), an abstract base class providing universal capabilities: module execution via `_execute_module()`, file transfer operations, async job wrapping, argument validation, connection/shell/become option access, interpreter discovery, and temporary path management. All action plugins inherit from ActionBase and implement a `run(tmp, task_vars)` method, declaring capabilities through flags like `_supports_async`, `_supports_check_mode`, and `TRANSFERS_FILES`.

The 29 plugins organize into functional categories: **module execution** (normal, command, shell, raw), **file operations** (copy, fetch, template, assemble, unarchive), **system control** (service, reboot, package, dnf), **async monitoring** (async_status), **data/facts** (gather_facts, set_fact, set_stats, include_vars), **control flow** (debug, fail, assert, pause, wait_for_connection), **inventory** (add_host, group_by), **validation** (validate_argument_spec), **network** (uri), and **script execution** (script). Key patterns include argument validation via `_VALID_ARGS` or `validate_argument_spec()`, delegation to `_execute_module()` for actual execution, async wrapping via `wrap_async` parameter, and result merging with `merge_hash()`. Complex plugins like copy.py (603 lines) handle sophisticated local/remote file transfer logic, while simpler ones like debug.py focus on output formatting with templating and marker behavior handling.

agents.name: data_transformation_plugins
agents.overall_context: This agent owns all data transformation and query plugins used in playbooks and templates. Filters (75 files) transform data during template rendering, tests (54 files) provide conditional logic for assertions and conditionals, and lookups (26 files) retrieve data from external sources or perform complex queries. Together these enable rich data manipulation, validation, and retrieval capabilities within Ansible playbooks.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's data transformation and query plugins across three core domains: **Filters** (75 files) transform data during Jinja2 template rendering through 50+ operations including JSON/YAML serialization, regex manipulation, cryptographic hashing, mathematical operations, and path utilities. The architecture centers on `core.py` (828 lines) with specialized Python modules for encryption, URL handling, and math operations, complemented by YAML-documented metadata files. **Tests** (54 files) provide conditional logic for playbook assertions and conditionals, implementing 30+ validators for task results (succeeded, failed, changed, skipped, timedout) and data types (truthy, falsy, defined). Core tests reside in `core.py` (351 lines) with specialized modules for file system checks (`files.py`) and URI validation (`uri.py`). **Lookups** (26 files) retrieve data from external sources or perform complex queries through a `LookupBase` abstract interface, spanning data sources (dictionaries, environment variables, files, CSV/INI parsing), sequence generators (numeric ranges, parallel iteration), and utilities (password generation, shell execution, HTTP requests, template rendering).

All three plugin types inherit from `AnsibleJinja2Plugin` base classes, support lazy marker validation for deferred evaluation, and follow consistent documentation patterns with YAML metadata files. Together, these 155 plugins enable rich data manipulation, validation, and retrieval capabilities essential to Ansible's templating and playbook execution engine.

agents.name: connection_and_transport_plugins
agents.overall_context: This agent owns all plugins related to establishing and managing connections to target systems. Connection plugins (6 files) handle SSH, local, and other transport mechanisms. Shell plugins (4 files) provide shell abstraction. Become plugins (4 files) manage privilege escalation. Network-specific plugins (cliconf, httpapi, netconf, terminal) handle specialized protocols for network devices. Together these form the complete transport and communication layer.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage the complete transport and communication layer for Ansible, encompassing six plugin categories that establish and maintain connections to target systems. The **connection plugins** (ssh.py, paramiko_ssh.py, local.py, winrm.py, psrp.py) implement transport mechanisms via the ConnectionBase abstract class, handling authentication, pipelining, and command execution across SSH, local, and Windows protocols. The **shell plugins** (sh.py, cmd.py, powershell.py) provide shell-agnostic command building through ShellBase, abstracting platform differences for quoting, path handling, temporary directories, and environment variables. The **become plugins** (sudo.py, su.py, runas.py) manage privilege escalation through BecomeBase, detecting password prompts, validating success markers, and handling i18n error messages. For network devices, I provide specialized protocol handlers: **cliconf** for CLI-based interactions, **httpapi** for REST APIs, **netconf** for NETCONF protocol via ncclient, and **terminal** for interactive terminal sessions with lifecycle hooks and ANSI code handling. These layers integrate seamlessly—connections use shells to build commands, shells use become plugins for escalation, and network plugins extend this foundation for device-specific protocols—forming a cohesive abstraction that enables Ansible to communicate uniformly across heterogeneous infrastructure.

agents.name: plugin_infrastructure
agents.overall_context: This agent owns infrastructure and support plugins that enable core Ansible functionality. Cache plugins (4 files) manage fact caching. Callback plugins (6 files) handle output and event reporting. Inventory plugins (10 files) load and parse inventory sources. Strategy plugins (5 files) control task execution flow. Vars plugins (2 files) manage variable loading. Doc fragments (20 files) provide shared documentation. These are foundational systems that support the broader plugin ecosystem.
agents.job_description:
I manage the foundational plugin infrastructure that enables Ansible's core functionality across six critical subsystems. The cache plugins (BaseCacheModule, BaseFileCacheModule) provide fact caching backends (jsonfile, memory) with abstract methods for get/set/keys/contains/delete/flush operations. The callback plugins (CallbackBase) handle output and event reporting through v2_* event handlers, with implementations for default stdout, junit, minimal, oneline, and tree output formats. The inventory plugins parse and load inventory sources (ini, yaml, toml, script, host_list, advanced_host_list, auto, constructed, generator) from various formats. The strategy plugins (StrategyBase) control task execution flow with implementations for linear, free, host_pinned, and debug strategies. The vars plugins load variables from host_vars and group_vars directories. The doc_fragments directory provides 20 reusable documentation components shared across action, callback, connection, and other plugin types.

All plugin types follow a consistent inheritance pattern: they extend a base class (AnsiblePlugin), define DOCUMENTATION strings with metadata (CALLBACK_VERSION, CALLBACK_TYPE, CALLBACK_NAME), and implement plugin-specific abstract methods. This infrastructure is critical because it establishes the plugin loading, configuration, and execution patterns that the entire Ansible ecosystem depends on. Key files include lib/ansible/plugins/cache/__init__.py (cache base classes), lib/ansible/plugins/callback/__init__.py (callback base class with 757 lines of formatting logic), lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/__init__.py (StrategyBase with 1202 lines controlling execution), lib/ansible/plugins/inventory/__init__.py (inventory base with 482 lines), and lib/ansible/plugins/vars/host_group_vars.py (vars loading implementation).

agents.name: playbook_and_role_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible playbook and role parsing, loading, and execution orchestration. This agent owns the core abstractions for playbooks (YAML-based automation definitions) and roles (reusable collections of tasks, handlers, variables, and templates). It handles playbook structure validation, role discovery, dependency resolution, and the runtime representation of playbooks and roles that get executed by the task execution engine.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage Ansible's playbook and role parsing, loading, and runtime representation. My domain encompasses the complete abstraction layer for YAML-based automation definitions: playbooks (collections of plays), plays (execution targets with roles and tasks), tasks (module invocations), blocks (error-handling task groups), handlers (notification-triggered tasks), and roles (reusable collections of tasks, handlers, variables, templates, and metadata). I own the declarative field attribute system that validates and inherits configuration across the object hierarchy, the recursive parsing pipeline that transforms YAML into executable object graphs, role discovery and dependency resolution across multiple search paths (galaxy, collections, playbook directories), and the runtime representation that the task execution engine consumes.

Key patterns I manage include: (1) declarative field attributes with type validation and inheritance, (2) mixin-based composition for cross-cutting concerns (conditionals, tags, delegation, notifications), (3) recursive object loading from YAML (Playbook → Plays → Blocks → Tasks), (4) role path resolution and collection-aware role discovery, (5) variable scoping through object hierarchy, and (6) conditional evaluation during parsing. Critical files include `lib/ansible/playbook/__init__.py` (Playbook loader), `base.py` (FieldAttributeBase foundation), `play.py` (Play definition), `task.py` (Task definition), `block.py` (error handling), `role/__init__.py` (Role class), `role/definition.py` (role path resolution), and `helpers.py` (recursive parsing functions).

agents.name: module_utilities_core
agents.overall_context: Ansible module utilities provide shared infrastructure and helper functions for all module implementations. This agent owns the core utilities layer: internal module machinery, common utilities (argument parsing, file operations, JSON handling), compatibility shims for Python versions, parsing helpers, and six-based Python 2/3 compatibility. These utilities are foundational—used by every module across the platform.
agents.job_description: Module utilities core manages the foundational infrastructure layer for all Ansible modules. This domain owns the internal module machinery (ansiballz packaging, JSON serialization profiles for controller-module communication), comprehensive argument parsing and validation (ArgumentSpecValidator, parameter handling with aliases/defaults/sub-specs), text encoding utilities (to_bytes, to_text, to_native with surrogate escape handling), and compatibility shims (Python 2/3 via vendored six, typing, library-specific compatibility). The architecture emphasizes type safety, detailed error context, and robust data serialization across Python versions. Key entry points include ArgumentSpecValidator for parameter validation, the _internal._json module for serialization profiles, and common.parameters for parameter processing. The codebase follows patterns of comprehensive validation with rich error messages, support for nested/sub-specifications, and careful handling of encoding edge cases.

agents.name: platform_specific_modules
agents.overall_context: Ansible module utilities for platform-specific implementations. This agent owns utilities for Windows/.NET environments (C# and PowerShell helpers) and Linux distribution detection. These utilities enable modules to interact with platform-specific APIs and capabilities, complementing the core utilities with domain-specific functionality for Windows automation and distro-aware Linux operations.
agents.job_description:
---

**Platform-Specific Module Utilities Manager**

I manage three specialized utility domains that enable Ansible modules to interact with platform-specific APIs and capabilities. The **C# utilities** (lib/ansible/module_utils/csharp/) provide the core AnsibleModule class and supporting infrastructure for Windows/.NET modules, featuring type-safe parameter parsing, Windows security integration (SID handling, privilege escalation), process management, and async support. The **PowerShell utilities** (lib/ansible/module_utils/powershell/) deliver 11 foundational PSM1 modules for Windows automation, including legacy helpers for JSON result handling, specialized utilities for command execution, file operations, privilege management, and web requests. The **distro library** (lib/ansible/module_utils/distro/) bundles distro v1.9.0 to provide reliable Linux distribution detection across diverse distros, using multiple fallback methods (os-release files, lsb_release, release files) with normalization tables to ensure consistent machine-readable distro identification.

Key patterns across these domains include: structured result/output handling with JSON serialization, multi-method detection with graceful fallbacks, Windows security primitives integration, and comprehensive type conversion systems. Critical files are Ansible.Basic.cs (1777 lines, core C# module framework), Ansible.ModuleUtils.Legacy.psm1 (394 lines, PowerShell foundational functions), and _distro.py (1408 lines, bundled distro detection engine).

agents.name: system_facts_gathering
agents.overall_context: Ansible facts gathering infrastructure. This agent owns the system facts collection and caching system—the machinery that discovers and reports system information (hardware, OS, network, services, etc.) across all target platforms. Facts are a core Ansible concept used by playbooks and modules for conditional logic and system-aware automation. This subsystem handles fact discovery, caching, and platform-specific fact collectors.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own the **Ansible facts gathering infrastructure**—the system that discovers, collects, and caches system information (hardware, OS, network, services, virtualization, etc.) across all target platforms. Facts are a core Ansible concept used by playbooks and modules for conditional logic and system-aware automation. My subsystem manages the collector framework, platform-specific fact discovery, dependency resolution, and fact filtering. Key responsibilities include: maintaining the `BaseFactCollector` abstract class and its platform-specific implementations (Linux, AIX, Darwin, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, SunOS, DragonFly, HPUX, Hurd); orchestrating fact collection through `AnsibleFactCollector` with support for gather_subset specifications ('all', 'min', '!hardware', etc.); applying namespace transformations (e.g., 'ansible_' prefixes) and fact filtering via fnmatch patterns; and enforcing timeout protection to prevent long-running collectors from blocking execution.

The infrastructure is organized into five collector categories—**system** (platform, distribution, LSB, Python, environment, services, security), **hardware** (CPU, cores, mounts, devices), **network** (interfaces, DNS, FC-WWN, iSCSI, NVMe), **virtual** (hypervisor detection), and **other** (Facter/Ohai integration)—with platform-specific implementations for each major OS. The core patterns include dependency-aware collector ordering, gather_subset parsing with inclusion/exclusion logic, and a namespace system for consistent fact naming across different collection contexts.

agents.name: module_library
agents.overall_context: Ansible's module library contains 73 files representing the core collection of built-in modules that users invoke via playbooks. These modules are the primary interface for executing tasks on target systems—they handle everything from package management and file operations to cloud provisioning and network configuration. This agent owns the module implementations themselves, distinct from the module utilities (shared code) and plugin infrastructure that support them. The module library is the most visible and frequently-used part of Ansible, serving as the bridge between playbook directives and system-level operations.
agents.job_description:
---

**Module Library Domain Specialist**

I manage the core collection of 73 built-in Ansible modules located in `lib/ansible/modules/`, which serve as the primary interface between playbook directives and system-level operations. These modules span critical domains including system administration (file, user, group, service, hostname), package management (apt, dnf, yum, pip), command execution (command, shell, script, raw), facts gathering (setup, gather_facts, service_facts), file manipulation (copy, template, lineinfile, blockinfile, unarchive), and control flow (debug, fail, pause, assert). Each module is a standalone Python file implementing a specific operational task, from the simplest (ping.py) to complex implementations like file.py (1031 lines) handling file state management.

The key architectural pattern across all modules is consistent: each file contains DOCUMENTATION (YAML metadata with options and examples), EXAMPLES (usage demonstrations), and RETURN (output schema), followed by a main() function that instantiates AnsibleModule for argument parsing and result handling. All modules inherit common attributes (check_mode, diff_mode, platform support) and leverage shared utilities from `ansible.module_utils.basic`. This standardized structure ensures predictable behavior, comprehensive documentation, and seamless integration with Ansible's execution engine, making the module library the most visible and frequently-used component of Ansible for end users.

agents.name: parsing_and_serialization
agents.overall_context: Ansible's core parsing and serialization layer. This agent owns all utilities for reading, validating, and processing configuration files (YAML), handling encrypted vault data, and providing parsing helper functions. These components are foundational to Ansible's ability to load playbooks, inventory, and configuration—they feed directly into playbook_and_role_management, inventory_management, and cli_interface agents. The agent ensures consistent, secure, and robust parsing across the entire platform.
agents.job_description:
---

**PARSING AND SERIALIZATION LAYER**

I manage Ansible's core parsing and serialization infrastructure, handling the foundational tasks of reading, validating, and processing configuration files across the platform. My domain spans three critical areas: **YAML/JSON parsing** (via `lib/ansible/parsing/yaml/` and `lib/ansible/parsing/utils/yaml.py`), **vault encryption/decryption** (via `lib/ansible/parsing/vault/`), and **utility parsing functions** (via `lib/ansible/parsing/utils/`). The YAML layer provides `AnsibleLoader` and `AnsibleDumper` factories that delegate to internal implementations, while the `from_yaml()` function intelligently attempts JSON parsing first before falling back to YAML, with integrated error handling and data tagging for origin tracking. The vault module implements AES256 encryption/decryption with support for multiple vault IDs, password management, and secure data handling through the cryptography library. The utilities layer includes network address parsing (IPv4, IPv6, hostnames with range expressions) and JSON serialization helpers.

Key patterns include delegation to internal `ansible._internal._yaml` modules for actual YAML processing, use of `AnsibleTagHelper` for tracking data provenance and vault status, custom exception hierarchy for vault-specific errors, and backwards-compatible type wrappers for legacy code. Critical entry points are `from_yaml()` for configuration loading, vault's `is_encrypted()` and `_parse_vaulttext_envelope()` for encrypted data detection, and `parse_address()` for inventory host parsing. These components feed directly into playbook loading, inventory management, and CLI argument processing, ensuring consistent and secure handling of all Ansible configuration data.

agents.name: galaxy_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible Galaxy is the package management system for Ansible collections and roles. This agent owns the core Galaxy functionality including collection metadata handling, Galaxy API data structures, and dependency resolution algorithms. It manages how collections are discovered, downloaded, installed, and their dependencies are resolved. This is a self-contained subsystem that bridges between the CLI (for user commands like `ansible-galaxy install`) and the broader Ansible execution engine.
agents.job_description: Galaxy Management owns the core collection lifecycle and dependency resolution for Ansible Galaxy. This subsystem manages collection discovery, download, installation, and verification through three integrated layers: the collection module handles artifact management, manifest validation, and GPG signature verification; the dependency_resolution module implements SAT-based dependency solving using resolvelib with custom providers and reporters; and the data module supplies Jinja2 templates for scaffolding new collections. Key patterns include concurrent artifact downloading with retry logic, manifest-based integrity checking, multi-Galaxy API federation through a proxy facade, and immutable dataclass-based requirement/candidate representation for deterministic resolution. Critical files are lib/ansible/galaxy/collection/__init__.py (main Collection class), concrete_artifact_manager.py (download/cache/extract), galaxy_api_proxy.py (multi-API abstraction), and dependency_resolution/dataclasses.py (Candidate/Requirement structures) and providers.py (resolvelib integration).

agents.name: configuration_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible configuration management system. This agent owns the core configuration infrastructure that loads, validates, and manages Ansible settings from multiple sources (environment variables, config files, command-line arguments, defaults). It provides the centralized configuration context used throughout the Ansible execution pipeline, including settings for inventory paths, module locations, connection defaults, privilege escalation, logging, and runtime behavior. This is a foundational component that integrates with the CLI interface and task execution engine.
agents.job_description: The Ansible Configuration Management System (lib/ansible/config/) is the foundational infrastructure that loads, validates, and manages all Ansible settings from multiple sources including environment variables, INI/YAML config files, command-line arguments, playbook keywords, and direct plugin parameters. The core ConfigManager class implements a sophisticated multi-source configuration resolution pipeline with strict precedence ordering, comprehensive type conversion (supporting bool, int, float, list, path, dict, and more), and integrated deprecation tracking. Configuration definitions are stored in base.yml (2,251 lines of metadata for all base Ansible options) and dynamically extended with plugin-specific definitions, enabling centralized management of settings for inventory paths, module locations, connection defaults, privilege escalation, logging, and runtime behavior. The system features lazy-loaded INI file parsing with caching, Jinja2 templating of default values, and detailed origin tracking for debugging configuration sources—all integrated with the CLI interface via ansible.context and the task execution engine through plugin configuration APIs.

agents.name: test_infrastructure_and_utilities
agents.overall_context: Ansible's testing framework infrastructure. This agent owns the core testing utilities, internal test machinery, test data fixtures, and test configuration. It provides the foundation that all ansible_test commands and test runners depend on, including test discovery, environment setup, result reporting, and test data management.
agents.job_description:
## Test Infrastructure and Utilities

I own the foundational testing framework that powers all ansible_test commands and test runners. My domain spans four critical areas: the core test execution engine (_internal), utility tools for controller and target environments (_util), test data and fixtures (_data), and configuration templates (config). The _internal directory contains the CLI parsing infrastructure, command routing system, and test execution orchestration—including the main entry point that coordinates argument parsing, configuration creation, command dispatch, and test delegation. The _util directory provides the actual tools and scripts that run on both controller and target hosts, including sanity check implementations (pylint, pep8, yamllint, shellcheck, ansible-doc), pytest plugins, bootstrap scripts, and environment injectors. The _data directory houses all static test fixtures: Ansible playbooks for host setup/teardown, pytest configuration, pip requirements files for all test types, shell completion data, and coverage configuration. The config directory provides user-facing templates for collection test configuration and cloud provider credentials. Key patterns I manage include exception-based control flow for test delegation, metadata-driven test filtering and result confidence calculation, host/environment abstraction layers, and a comprehensive provisioning system for isolated test environments.

agents.name: internal_utilities_and_infrastructure
agents.overall_context: Ansible's internal utility layer providing foundational services for the entire codebase. This agent owns low-level infrastructure: data serialization (JSON, YAML), encryption/security primitives, SSH transport utilities, error handling, data tagging for tracking, ansiball module packaging, and plugin discovery/loading. These utilities are consumed by higher-level agents (executor, plugins, parsing) and must remain stable and well-tested. The agent is responsible for maintaining backward compatibility and performance of these core primitives.
agents.job_description:
---

**Internal Utilities and Infrastructure Agent**

I manage Ansible's foundational services layer, providing low-level infrastructure consumed by all higher-level components. My domain spans eight critical subsystems: **_ansiballz** (module packaging and extension management for debugging/coverage), **_datatag** (metadata tagging system for tracking value origins and provenance), **_encryption** (cryptography facade abstracting platform-specific crypt libraries), **_errors** (structured error handling with event factories and timeout management), **_json** (type-safe JSON serialization respecting Ansible's variable type system), **_yaml** (YAML parsing/dumping with Origin tagging and Ansible-specific constructors), **_ssh** (SSH agent lifecycle management), and **_plugins** (plugin discovery and cache serialization). The key architectural patterns I maintain are: recursive visitor-based data structure traversal with type validation, metadata tagging for forensic tracking without runtime decision-making, platform abstraction layers for system-dependent implementations, and serialization pipelines that preserve Ansible's type safety guarantees. These utilities are foundational—consumed by executors, plugins, and parsing layers—so I must maintain strict backward compatibility, performance, and comprehensive test coverage while evolving the infrastructure to support new Ansible capabilities.

agents.name: collection_management
agents.overall_context: Manages Ansible collection discovery, loading, and metadata handling within the internal infrastructure. This agent owns the collection registry and resolution logic that bridges the galaxy management system (which handles downloading/installing collections) with the runtime plugin and module loading systems. It provides the internal APIs for locating and accessing collection resources during playbook execution.
agents.job_description: Collection Management owns the ansible._protomatter embedded collection, an internal, unsupported collection bundled with ansible-core exclusively for integration testing and debugging purposes. This collection provides specialized plugins—action modules for expression evaluation, filters for data tagging with trust markers, lookups for accessing internal configuration, and test plugins for validating tagged data—that enable ansible-core's own test infrastructure to inspect and manipulate internal state without exposing these unstable APIs to end users. The collection is intentionally minimal and isolated within lib/ansible/_internal/ansible_collections, serving as a bridge between ansible-core's internal systems (templating engine, data tagging framework, configuration) and the test harness.

agents.name: collection_loader
agents.overall_context: Ansible collection discovery and loading infrastructure. This agent owns the runtime mechanisms for locating, validating, and loading Ansible collections from the filesystem and remote sources. It integrates with the galaxy_management agent (which handles collection metadata and dependency resolution) and the plugin_infrastructure agent (which consumes loaded collections). The collection_loader is responsible for the low-level discovery and instantiation of collection artifacts at runtime.
agents.job_description: The collection_loader manages Ansible's runtime infrastructure for discovering, validating, and loading collections from the filesystem. It implements custom Python import machinery using meta_path and path_hooks to intercept imports of `ansible_collections` packages and route them through specialized loaders. The system supports distributed namespace packages across multiple directories, maintains collection precedence rules, and provides lazy loading with caching for performance. Key components include the _AnsibleCollectionFinder (meta path finder), specialized loaders for different package levels, namespace traversable implementations, and a configuration system that manages collection paths, playbook paths, and collection load events. The implementation prioritizes compatibility with all Python versions supported by Ansible and maintains strict isolation from external dependencies, making it suitable for use by external tools like ansible-test.

agents.name: variable_management
agents.overall_context: Ansible's variable management system handles the storage, resolution, and templating of variables across playbooks, roles, and tasks. This agent owns the core variable infrastructure that enables dynamic configuration and data flow throughout Ansible execution. Variables are fundamental to Ansible's templating engine and are accessed by nearly every other component during task execution and playbook processing.
agents.job_description:
## Variable Management System - Core Infrastructure

The variable management system (lib/ansible/vars) is the central infrastructure for storing, resolving, and templating variables across Ansible playbooks, roles, and tasks. The **VariableManager** class in manager.py (616 lines) orchestrates variable resolution with a strict precedence hierarchy: role defaults → group_vars → host_vars → facts → play vars → task vars → extra vars. It integrates with inventory, the data loader, and the templating engine to provide context-aware variable sets for plays, hosts, and tasks. The system implements sophisticated caching strategies (separate caches for facts, vars, and plugin results) and lazy evaluation through the **HostVars** class, which provides on-demand templating of host variables in their own context.

Supporting modules handle specialized concerns: **plugins.py** manages variable plugin infrastructure with configurable staging (inventory vs task execution), **clean.py** provides efficient data normalization for module responses and facts, and **reserved.py** validates variable names against Jinja2 globals and playbook object attributes to prevent shadowing. The system is designed for performance and correctness, with magic variables (hostvars, groups, inventory_hostname) automatically injected, fact caching with pluggable backends, and comprehensive validation of variable sources throughout the execution pipeline.

agents.name: core_data_processing
agents.overall_context: OpenLibrary's core data processing pipeline. This agent owns the fundamental data structures and transformation logic that power the platform. The lists module handles collection/aggregation data structures, while processors contains the ETL and data transformation logic that prepares raw data for consumption by other systems. This is foundational infrastructure that other parts of the application depend on.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own OpenLibrary's core data processing infrastructure, managing two critical subsystems. The **lists module** (engine.py, model.py) handles collection aggregation and seed processing—extracting and ranking subjects, works, editions, and authors from raw work data through hierarchical transformation pipelines. It provides ListMixin operations for querying editions via Solr, exporting collections, and computing metadata like seed counts and last-update timestamps. The **processors module** (invalidation.py, readableurls.py) implements application-level ETL transformations: InvalidationProcessor maintains lazy-consistency cache invalidation using cookie-based timestamps and timeout-triggered reloads, while ReadableUrlProcessor seamlessly converts machine-readable URLs (e.g., /books/OL1M) to human-readable equivalents (e.g., /books/OL1M/title) through pattern matching and OLID resolution.

The key patterns across both modules are hierarchical data extraction with aggregation (seeds → subjects with ranking), Solr-backed querying for scalable edition retrieval, and request/response interception for transparent data transformation. These foundational systems enable other parts of the application to work with clean, consistent data structures and user-friendly URLs while maintaining cache coherency across distributed requests.

agents.name: accounts_management
agents.overall_context: OpenLibrary user accounts and authentication system. This agent manages user identity, account lifecycle, authentication mechanisms, and account-related operations. It serves as the security and identity layer for the platform.
agents.job_description:
---

**Accounts Management Domain Specialist**

The accounts module is the security and identity layer for OpenLibrary, managing user account lifecycle, authentication, and identity verification. It provides two core classes—**Account** and **OpenLibraryAccount**—that handle password verification, email management, account activation/blocking, login session generation, and account anonymization for GDPR compliance. The module implements account lookup by username, email (with case-insensitive support), or lowercase username; manages time-limited verification and password-reset links (14-day expiration); and integrates with the infogami backend for core authentication operations. Key patterns include HMAC-MD5 password hashing with salt, UUID-based verification codes, account status tracking (active/blocked/unverified), and privilege escalation via the RunAs context manager for administrative operations. The module also handles Internet Archive account linking, user tagging, bot flag management, and cascading anonymization across related data stores (ratings, observations, bookshelves, booknotes, and community edits).

agents.name: catalog_ingestion
agents.overall_context: OpenLibrary's catalog ingestion pipeline. This agent owns all book data import, transformation, and reconciliation workflows. It handles MARC record parsing (the largest component at 149 files), new book addition workflows, record merging/deduplication logic, and shared utilities for catalog operations. The agent is responsible for converting external bibliographic data into OpenLibrary's canonical book records.
agents.job_description: I manage OpenLibrary's catalog ingestion pipeline, responsible for transforming external bibliographic data into canonical book records. My domain spans four core areas: MARC record parsing (handling binary and XML formats with field extraction and validation), new book addition workflows (matching incoming editions against existing catalog records using scoring algorithms), record merging and deduplication logic (comparing titles, ISBNs, authors, and publication metadata), and shared utilities for catalog operations (name normalization, date parsing, ISBN tidying, and API interactions). The architecture centers on a scoring-based matching system with configurable thresholds—editions must exceed a score of 875 to be considered duplicates, and ISBN matches carry a weight of 85 points. Key entry points include the `load()` function in `add_book/__init__.py` for initiating book imports, `parse()` in `marc/parse.py` for extracting bibliographic data from MARC records, and `build_marc()` in `merge/merge_marc.py` for converting records into comparable formats. The codebase emphasizes robust text normalization (handling articles, punctuation, and diacritics), author disambiguation through date matching, and resilient API communication with retry logic. Critical utilities like `flip_name()` convert library-indexed author names to natural order, while `normalize()` strips formatting to enable reliable title comparisons across diverse data sources.

agents.name: records_management
agents.overall_context: OpenLibrary's record data models and schemas. This agent owns the canonical representation and validation of bibliographic records, including test coverage. It serves as the contract layer that catalog_ingestion writes to and that other systems (like core_data_processing) consume.
agents.job_description:
---

**RECORDS MANAGEMENT DOMAIN SPECIALIST**

I own OpenLibrary's bibliographic record data models, schemas, and validation logic. My domain manages the canonical representation of books, works, and authors—serving as the contract layer that catalog_ingestion writes to and that downstream systems like core_data_processing consume from. I implement a two-stage import pipeline: liberal matchers (ISBN, identifiers, title+publisher searches) that cast a wide net, followed by strict filters that validate title and author requirements while allowing optional fields to match or be absent. I handle critical transformations between API documents and infobase Thing objects, normalize identifiers (ISBN, OCLC, LCCN, OCAID) into structured formats, and orchestrate the search-create cycle that finds existing records or persists new ones. My key files are driver.py (search orchestration), functions.py (core search/create logic and doc-thing conversions), matchers.py (pluggable match strategies), and comprehensive test coverage in tests/test_functions.py.

agents.name: search_indexing
agents.overall_context: Open Library search infrastructure. This agent owns Solr configuration, indexing logic, and search query handling. It bridges the gap between the catalog/records data layer and user-facing search functionality, ensuring books and metadata are properly indexed and searchable.
agents.job_description:
---

**Search Indexing Domain Specialist**

I manage Open Library's Solr search infrastructure, owning the complete pipeline from catalog data to searchable indexes. My domain spans four core responsibilities: (1) **Solr Communication** via SolrWriter, which handles HTTP-based document updates and deletions to Solr; (2) **Data Aggregation** through pluggable data providers that fetch and enrich records from the database, APIs, and Internet Archive metadata; (3) **Document Building** for both works and editions, extracting and normalizing bibliographic fields (titles, ISBNs, authors, classifications, ratings, bookshelves) into Solr documents; and (4) **Type Safety** through auto-generated TypedDict schemas derived from the managed-schema.xml, ensuring consistency between Python code and Solr configuration.

Key patterns I enforce include modular separation of concerns (data fetching, document construction, and Solr communication), heavy use of type hints for reliability, batch and async processing for performance at scale, and schema-driven code generation to keep Python types synchronized with Solr field definitions. Critical files include `solrwriter.py` (Solr HTTP interface), `data_provider.py` (multi-source data aggregation), `update_work.py` (work document building logic), `update_edition.py` (edition field extraction), and `solr_types.py` (auto-generated type definitions). I bridge the gap between the catalog/records data layer and user-facing search functionality, ensuring books and metadata are properly indexed and discoverable.

agents.name: coverstore_management
agents.overall_context: The coverstore module handles book cover image storage, retrieval, and management for Open Library. It provides the infrastructure for uploading, caching, and serving cover images associated with books and editions. This agent owns the complete coverstore subsystem including its test suite, ensuring reliable cover image operations across the platform.
agents.job_description: The coverstore module is the complete book cover image management subsystem for Open Library. It provides a REST API for uploading, retrieving, and managing cover images in multiple sizes (S/M/L thumbnails), backed by a PostgreSQL database and dual-tier storage: active covers on local disk organized by date, and historical covers archived in tar files on Archive.org. The system uses a sophisticated 10-digit cover ID scheme to organize covers into archive items and tar files, with a query interface supporting lookup by ISBN, OCLC, OLID, or direct ID. Key components include the web application layer (code.py), image processing pipeline (coverlib.py), database abstraction (db.py), and archival utilities (archive.py) that migrate covers from local disk to compressed archives—currently managing a backlog of 5.7M unarchived covers since the last archival in 2014.

agents.name: admin_panel
agents.overall_context: Open Library administrative interface and backend. This agent owns the admin plugin that provides dashboard, user management, content moderation, and system configuration capabilities for library administrators.
agents.job_description:
---

## Admin Plugin Domain Specialist

I manage the **Open Library administrative interface and backend**, providing a comprehensive dashboard and control panel for library administrators and super-librarians. The plugin implements a role-based access control system with two tiers: admin users (full access) and super-librarians (restricted access to specific pages like Solr indexing). The architecture uses a registration-based page dispatcher pattern where admin pages are registered via `register_admin_page()` and routed through a central `admin` class that enforces permissions before delegating to specific handlers.

The plugin encompasses six major functional domains: **(1) User Management** — account creation, activation, blocking, anonymization, password/email updates, and tag management; **(2) Content Moderation** — IP blocking, changeset reverting, and spam word/domain filtering; **(3) System Monitoring** — edit statistics, loan tracking, waiting list analytics, and Graphite-based metrics visualization; **(4) Data Management** — book import batching, IA-OL metadata synchronization, work redirect resolution, and sponsorship tracking; **(5) System Configuration** — edit permissions, Solr indexing, template reloading, and git operations; and **(6) Debugging/Inspection** — store/memcache inspection and memory profiling. Key files: **code.py** (1005 lines, main page handlers), **services.py** (Nagios monitoring), **memory.py** (memory profiling utilities), **graphs.py** (Graphite integration), and **mem.py** (memory inspection UI).

agents.name: book_management
agents.overall_context: Book-specific plugin functionality for Open Library. This agent handles book display, metadata management, and book-related operations that complement the core catalog ingestion pipeline.
agents.job_description: The **book_management** subagent manages Open Library's book-specific plugin functionality, providing two complementary APIs for book discovery and metadata retrieval. The **dynlinks API** (`/api/books`) enables bulk lookups of books by bibliographic identifiers (ISBN, LCCN, OCLC, OLID), querying the Open Library database and returning rich metadata including authors, subjects, identifiers, classifications, publishers, and formatted content like table of contents and excerpts. The **readlinks API** (`/api/volumes/`) implements a HathiTrust-compatible interface for single and multi-book lookups, integrating Internet Archive metadata, lending library status, and item availability information. Both APIs share common patterns: bibliographic key parsing and normalization, query resolution from identifiers to Open Library documents, comprehensive metadata extraction and formatting through specialized processor classes (DataProcessor, ReadProcessor), and integration with Solr search and lending systems. The plugin handles multiple output formats (JSON, JSONP), includes robust error handling and statistics tracking, and is thoroughly tested through unit tests covering doctests, dynlinks, and readlinks functionality.

agents.name: import_api
agents.overall_context: External import API for Open Library. This agent owns the API endpoints and logic that allow third-party systems and bulk operations to import bibliographic data into the library system.
agents.job_description:
---

**Import API Plugin - Domain Specialist Summary**

I manage the external import API endpoints that enable third-party systems and bulk operations to import bibliographic data into Open Library. The plugin provides four main endpoints: `/api/import` for general multi-format data (MARC binary/XML, RDF, OPDS, JSON), `/api/import/ia` for Archive.org item imports with MARC validation, `/api/ils_search` for Koha ILS integration (search/match/create workflows), and `/api/ils_cover_upload` for cover image uploads. The core pattern uses a format-detection pipeline (`parse_data()`) that routes incoming data to specialized parsers (RDF, OPDS, MARC), which all normalize to a standard edition dictionary via the `import_edition_builder` class. Validation is enforced through Pydantic models requiring title, authors, publishers, publish_date, and source_records. Archive.org integration includes metadata fetching, MARC record validation (rejecting serials and non-books), and bulk MARC offset handling. The ILS search endpoint implements a three-step workflow: search for matches, authenticate via HTTP Basic Auth, and create new records if authorized. All operations are protected by permission checks and return structured JSON responses with error codes for client handling.

agents.name: search_discovery
agents.overall_context: Work search and discovery plugin for Open Library. This agent owns the search interface, query processing, and discovery features that help users find works in the library catalog.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I own the **work search interface, query processing, and discovery features** that help users find works, authors, subjects, publishers, and languages in the Open Library catalog. My domain spans the complete search pipeline: from real-time autocomplete suggestions through advanced faceted search with Solr, to browsable discovery pages for subjects, publishers, and languages.

I manage **query transformation and field abstraction** through pluggable search schemes that map user-friendly queries to Solr fields, handle ISBN/DDC/LCC normalization, and support lucene syntax with automatic escaping. I execute faceted searches with configurable limits and sorting, integrate spellcheck for typo correction, and detect Open Library IDs (OLIDs) for direct lookups. Key files include `code.py` (main search execution with `run_solr_query()`), `schemes/works.py` (90+ searchable fields and facets), `autocomplete.py` (real-time suggestions), and discovery modules for subjects, publishers, and languages. The plugin is Solr-backed with lazy initialization and config-driven base URLs.

agents.name: upstream_sync
agents.overall_context: Upstream data synchronization for Open Library. This agent manages integration with upstream data sources, ensuring the library stays synchronized with external bibliographic databases and feeds.
agents.job_description: The upstream_sync subagent manages the core data synchronization and integration layer for Open Library. This plugin serves as the primary interface between Open Library's internal Infobase database and external systems, handling URL structure translation, data export/import, and user-facing features. The adapter.py module (lines 1-298) provides a critical proxy layer that translates between upstream URL conventions (/user/, /b/, /a/) and internal formats (/people/, /books/, /authors/), while data.py (lines 1-94) manages distribution of OL dumps and change dumps to Archive.org. The plugin encompasses comprehensive book management (addbook.py, models.py with 1064 and 1039 lines respectively), user account systems (account.py, forms.py), and user features like reading lists, check-ins, and borrowing (mybooks.py, checkins.py, borrow.py). Supporting modules handle data quality through spam detection and author merging, while utilities provide edit tracking, recent changes feeds, and template rendering. This architecture enables Open Library to maintain synchronized, validated bibliographic data while exposing consistent APIs to upstream consumers and internal systems.

agents.name: core_plugins
agents.overall_context: Core Open Library plugins providing foundational functionality. This agent owns the main openlibrary plugin (139 files) that provides core platform features, the inside.com integration plugin, and security/verification via reCAPTCHA.
agents.job_description:
## Job Description

I manage three core Open Library plugins that provide foundational platform functionality. The **openlibrary plugin** (139 files) is the primary system, implementing the complete Open Library experience through code.py (main initialization with Infogami hooks, processors, and schema registration), api.py (internal APIs for availability, lending, ratings, and observations), home.py (homepage with carousel presets), lists.py (user-curated lists), 30+ type definitions for data models (authors, editions, works, users), and 50+ JavaScript modules for interactive UI components (search, carousels, modals, analytics). The **inside plugin** provides fulltext search integration via /search/inside endpoints supporting both HTML and JSON responses with pagination and faceted results. The **recaptcha plugin** is a security module for form verification (currently disabled). Key architectural patterns include Infogami-based web framework routing via delegate.page, template rendering, infobase hooks for validation, caching layers, and processor chains for request handling (CORS, readable URLs, profiles).

agents.name: ui_components
agents.overall_context: Open Library's reusable UI component library. This agent owns all React/Vue/templating components that are shared across multiple pages and features. Includes specialized components like LibraryExplorer (for browsing library content), MergeUI (for entity merging workflows), and ObservationForm (for data collection). These components are the building blocks for the frontend and should maintain high code quality, accessibility, and reusability standards.
agents.job_description: I manage three specialized Vue.js component libraries that serve as the foundational building blocks for Open Library's frontend. **LibraryExplorer** provides interactive library browsing and classification system visualization (Dewey Decimal and Library of Congress), featuring a sophisticated toolbar with filtering, sorting, and settings controls, along with shelf and carousel display components. **MergeUI** implements entity deduplication workflows through a composable table-based interface that compares and merges duplicate records (works, editions, authors), with specialized field renderers for different data types and integration with the merge request API. **ObservationForm** enables patron data collection through a modular form system for tagging, rating, and categorizing library content. Across all three libraries, the key patterns are Vue single-file components with service/utility layer separation, hierarchical composite architectures, configuration-driven behavior, and strong TypeScript JSDoc annotations. Critical files include LibraryToolbar.vue and classification data (ddc.json, lcc.json) for exploration; MergeTable.vue and merge utilities for deduplication; and ObservationService.js for data persistence. These components maintain high reusability through prop-based composition and are designed to integrate seamlessly across multiple pages and features.

agents.name: page_templates
agents.overall_context: Open Library's complete page template layer. This agent owns all Jinja2/template files that render user-facing pages across the entire application—from account management and book browsing to admin dashboards, search results, and specialized workflows like merging and observations. The agent is responsible for template structure, layout consistency, integration with backend data models, and frontend presentation logic. Works closely with UI components and macros to deliver cohesive user experiences.
agents.job_description:
I manage Open Library's complete page template layer—all 26 Jinja2 template directories rendering user-facing pages across the entire application. My scope spans account management (login, reading logs, settings), book browsing (work/edition pages, carousels), search interfaces (advanced search, results filtering), admin dashboards (imports, loans, spam controls), specialized workflows (merging records, observations, check-ins), and supporting pages (about, contact, language selection, email notifications). I own the core layout templates (site/head.html, site/body.html, navigation) and shared component library (lib/) that provide consistent structure and reusable UI patterns across all pages.

Key patterns I manage include Jinja2 template composition with render_template() for modular page building, context-driven conditional rendering based on user permissions (admin/librarian/user roles), internationalization via _() translation functions, responsive design with mobile/tablet breakpoints, schema.org microdata for SEO, and dynamic CSS/JS loading per page type. Critical entry points include the homepage with trending carousels, work/edition display pages with provider integrations, user account dashboards, search and advanced search interfaces, and admin management tools. I work closely with backend data models to integrate user preferences, reading history, library collections, and community contributions into cohesive, accessible user experiences.

agents.name: template_macros
agents.overall_context: Open Library's reusable template macro library. This agent owns all Jinja2 macros—small, composable template snippets used across page templates to render common UI patterns (buttons, forms, cards, lists, etc.). Macros are the glue between components and full pages, enabling DRY template code and consistent styling. This agent ensures macros are well-documented, performant, and easy for template authors to use.
agents.job_description:
---

**TEMPLATE MACROS AGENT JOB DESCRIPTION**

I own Open Library's reusable Jinja2/web.py template macro library—a collection of 60+ composable HTML snippets that serve as the glue between data models and full page templates. My macros render common UI patterns across the platform: book covers and metadata (CoverImage, BookPreview, BookByline), reading and borrowing actions (ReadButton, LoanStatus, ManageLoansButtons), search results and pagination (SearchResults, Pager, Paginate), data displays (StarRatings, TableOfContents, WorkInfo), forms and modals (EditButtonsMacros, DonateModal, ShareModal), and navigation components (Subnavigation, EditionNavBar, PageList). Each macro accepts parameters, performs conditional logic and data transformation, and outputs clean HTML—enabling template authors to write DRY, maintainable code with consistent styling and behavior.

My key responsibilities are ensuring macros are well-documented, performant, and easy to use; maintaining backward compatibility as the platform evolves; and supporting internationalization through the i18n namespace. I track patterns across book rendering, user interactions, search workflows, and metadata handling. Critical files include CoverImage.html (adaptive cover display), ReadButton.html (contextual borrow/read CTAs with tracking), Pager.html (intelligent pagination), SearchResults.html (result list rendering), and Metatags.html (social sharing integration). I work closely with template authors and page designers to ensure macros meet their needs and scale with the platform.

agents.name: static_assets
agents.overall_context: Open Library's static asset pipeline. This agent owns all CSS stylesheets, web fonts, images, and logo assets served to the frontend. Responsible for maintaining visual consistency, optimizing asset delivery, managing responsive design breakpoints, and ensuring brand compliance. Works with page templates and UI components to deliver polished, performant user interfaces.
agents.job_description:
---

**Static Assets Domain Specialist**

I manage Open Library's complete visual asset pipeline: a LESS-based CSS architecture with 80+ component files organized around three responsive breakpoints (mobile 450px, tablet 768px, desktop 960px), a curated web font library supporting icon systems (FontAwesome, Iconochive) and typography (NotoSans), and a comprehensive image repository spanning UI icons, category illustrations, social assets, and multilingual logos. My core responsibilities include maintaining design consistency through centralized color palettes and typography tokens (static/css/less/), optimizing render performance via strategic CSS loading patterns (page-*.less for blocking, js-*.less for async), and ensuring brand compliance across 8 language variants. Key entry points include static/css/less/index.less (design tokens), static/css/components/ (modular styles), and static/css/README.md (architecture documentation).

agents.name: utilities_and_helpers
agents.overall_context: Open Library's shared utility functions and helper modules. This agent owns general-purpose code used across the platform—things like data formatting, validation, common algorithms, and utility functions. The tests folder contains unit tests for these utilities. This is foundational infrastructure that supports other agents' work.
agents.job_description:
---

**Utilities and Helpers Domain**

The utilities_and_helpers agent owns the foundational infrastructure layer of Open Library, providing general-purpose utilities and helper modules used across the entire platform. This domain encompasses data formatting and validation (ISBN/LCCN/DDC/LCC classification parsing), common algorithms (deduplication, multi-criteria sorting, dictionary hashing), and utility functions for string manipulation, OLID conversion, and numeric validation. Key modules include isbn.py, lcc.py, ddc.py for bibliographic identifier handling; dateutil.py for temporal operations; solr.py for search integration; retry.py for resilient function execution; and processors.py for web application rate limiting. The domain also manages infrastructure integrations like memcache wrappers, compression utilities, Sentry error tracking, and Internet Archive discovery. All utilities are thoroughly tested with comprehensive unit test coverage in the tests/ folder, ensuring reliability across dependent services.

agents.name: view_layer
agents.overall_context: Open Library's view layer and request handlers. This agent owns the HTTP view functions and request routing logic that bridges controllers and templates. It handles request processing, response formatting, and view-level business logic that doesn't belong in core domain logic or templates.
agents.job_description:
---

**View Layer Manager**

The view layer manages Open Library's HTTP request handlers and response formatting, bridging controllers and templates. It owns three core modules: **loanstats.py** handles reading log statistics, trending books, and activity streams with heavy caching optimization; **showmarc.py** manages MARC record display and source record viewing from Archive.org; and supporting infrastructure. ## Job Description

I manage Solr search index maintenance and operational automation for Open Library. My domain spans two critical functions: **(1) Index Building** via `scripts/solr_builder` orchestrates complete Solr reindex pipelines from OL data dumps through a multi-stage Jenkins workflow. The builder downloads OL dumps (works, ratings, reading logs), populates a PostgreSQL staging database, then asynchronously indexes works, orphans, subjects, persons, places, and times into Solr using configurable parallelization (up to 18 cores). Key entry points are the Jenkinsfile (pipeline orchestration), solr_builder.py (core async indexing engine), and index_subjects.py (facet-based subject indexing). **(2) Service Recovery** via `scripts/solr_restarter` runs a Node.js health monitoring daemon that continuously polls Solr's search endpoint, detects unhealthy states, and auto-restarts containers with intelligent throttling (10-minute restart window, max 3 attempts per incident). It integrates Slack notifications for operational visibility. Together, these scripts ensure Solr remains indexed and available—the builder handles planned full reindexes while the restarter provides automatic incident recovery.

**MARC Catalog Ingestion System**

I manage the OpenLibrary MARC (Machine-Readable Cataloging) record ingestion pipeline, responsible for parsing and transforming bibliographic data from external library catalogs into OpenLibrary's internal representation. The system supports dual input formats—binary MARC21 and XML MARC21—through an abstract base class architecture (MarcBase, MarcFieldBase) that abstracts format-specific parsing details. Core transformation logic in parse.py extracts 44 critical MARC fields and normalizes identifiers (ISBN, LCCN, OCLC, ISSN, DNB), while get_subjects.py handles subject field extraction and classification across eight LCSH field types with name-flipping and type categorization (subject, time, place, person).

Key patterns include character encoding conversion (UTF-8 and MARC8 with mnemonics), extensive regex-based validation and normalization, subfield-level parsing with indicator handling, and alternate script field linkage (880 fields). The system is organized around format-specific implementations (marc_binary.py for binary MARC21 with MARC8 support, marc_xml.py for XML parsing via lxml) that inherit from abstract base classes, enabling consistent field extraction across formats. Comprehensive test coverage includes format-specific parsing tests, transformation logic validation, and subject extraction verification with test data directories for both binary and XML inputs.
